comments.name: Don't ask
comments.body: While I sympathize with the frustration, the fact is that most analysts saw that Spirit's operating model as unsustainable, regardless of what credit cards they did or didn't have. A good comparison is Alaska, which launched a popular travel CC with VISA several years ago despite being a relatively small airline at the time. They've been remarkably successful despite that. However, their model looks a lot more like a full service airline, and they were more focused on building a fortress in a relatively undeserved market rather than trying to compete head on with the big four. Another counterpoint is bank-issued travel cards, which offer similar benefits to an airline CC but don't tie you to a specific airline. We've had one for several years and find it easily pays for itself. I suspect the main reason large banks wouldn't work with Spirit was because it served a customer base they weren't interested in serving.

comments.name: Keith
comments.body: Another key factor here is that the currency of airline specific frequent flier miles creates loyalty for the banks with those exclusive cobranded cards (AMEX, Chase and Citi).  That loyalty comes at a price.  If you want a card that earns miles for your preferred airline you are likely to be paying an annual fee to the credit card company for the privilege to have your "rewards" in your preferred form of currency.  What happens if/when the airlines devalue what a mile is worth, because it will happen at some point?

comments.name: Dan
comments.body: We need to think about frequent flyer programs differently: they are no longer about rewarding loyalty, they are about pre-selling seats. Not unlike large corporate contracts, with minimum purchase guarantees (whether all the seats are used or not). Airlines function more as pseudo-central banks, issuing a currency backed by an asset (travel). Actual banks (and others) have pseudo-inter-bank relationships with airlines. When you look at it this way, the system makes more sense: only those able to back a "currency" have the ability to issue one, and few carriers have enough seats, destinations, and infrastructure to backstop this one. It may not make the system fair, but at least it provides a better understanding of it.

We had to go a very long distance in the airport to reach our second flight. I reached the gate as they were about to close the door. I told them my two companions would arrive any minute. The agent was rude and told me he couldn't hold the plane for a single person. I argued with him (to give my companions some more time). Bottom line, the airline caused the problem and yet did virtually nothing to make sure we got to our destination. comments.name: Jim Johnson
comments.body:
Booking out bound and your return flight separately is a good idea.  If you book out and back on one ticket once you take the first flight on the out bound it become difficult to change the return flight.  If you need to come back early or decide you would like to stay longer it is difficult/costly to change the return part of the ticket.

Sometime prices will drop at the last minute. It doesn't happen often but when it does you can do very well.

My wife and I flew to Europe this summer. I started following the ticket prices  for the return while we were there.  Found the same flight back from Paris 3 days later at a much lower price. Cancelled the return ticket, got and e-credit, booked the later flight using part of the e-credit. The remaining e-credit which I'll use on my next flight is about the same as what we paid for 3 nights hotel in Paris.  The later flight was so empty we got upgraded to business class, haven't seen a flight that empty in 10 years, whole rows empty in Economy. 

A couple of years ago we were in Vietnam.  Again was checking return prices while we were there. About a week before we were coming back found a great deal on another airline. Booked the other carrier was about $1,500 cheaper.  Canceled our tickets, used the e-credit later.

Let me add my story: This summer we flew from Europe back to the US. The scheduled flight was on United to Newark Intl. Airport.
After waiting several hours at the gate, we finally learned that a part for our plane ( a Boeing of course! Check out the recent Netflix docs) was permanently broken and had now be flown in from the UK or the Netherlands- they weren’t quite sure.
Because this was a code share flight with Lufthansa, United pushed the responsibility of rebooking everyone onto Lufthansa personnel who worked diligently over several hours to get people rebooked. Not a single United rep showed their face or apologized during that time at all.
We managed to get on a Lufthansa flight ( on the world largest airplane - an Airbus) and managed to get to Dulles airport with a delay of 7 hours and took a rental car back home. 
Now - and here is were policy and the law makes a difference - we immediately submitted compensation claims under EU law for undue flight delays, documented everything carefully and already have received a payment of 600 Euros per person plus the cost of the rental from United! If the U S had a similar policy and a duty to reimburse airline customers for undue delays, I am positive that air travel would improve and also get safer and more efficient again! It‘s in our hands and doesn’t take a genius to implement - just some consumer rights and human decency!

Coming to an interview slurping a latte, carrying a condensation-drenched cold drink cup by 2-fingers, or munching food ... 

Sorry ... you're showing the interviewer as much disrespect as showing up in torn shorts, flip-flops, and a "muscle" T-shirt or bikini top. It doesn't show 'rebellion against conformity"; it shows a distinct lack of consideration and judgement, especially toward your not-to-be boss.

I wish people would understand just how much our $40 trillion debt is. 
Here is an image. Take $100 bills, make a stack of ten. Thats a thousand. Now make a thousand stacks of those. Thats a million. So now you have 1000 stacks of ten $100 bills. Clearly not enough, so stack those all together. Now you have one stack of hundred dollar bills- that totals a million. Make a thousand stacks just like that. So now you have 1000 stacks of a million dollars. Now you have a billion. Shoot- still not enough. Ok, take that 1000 stacks of a million dollars each stack and pile it all together. Thats a pile of a billion dollars. Now you need 1000 stacks of that- 1000 stacks of a billion follars each stack. Now you have a trillion. Which is less than 1/40 of our debt. 
A stack of $100 bills, which are less than half a hundredth of an inch wide, would go up over 27 MILES to equal our debt.

comments.name: MattZN
comments.body:
The problem we face as a society is that debt... and mortgage debt in particular, is a self-reinforcing rabbit hole that makes the vast majority of the people poorer.  It is sold as improving affordability, but it is actually a direct transfer of wealth from poorer people to wealthier people and always has been.

All else being equal, rising mortgage rates are the only way for this rabbit hole to correct.   Home prices in absolute terms drop and people are forced to save more money to increase their up-front down-payment.  This reduces the money transfer from the larger society to the rich.  It may not seem that way, but that is what happens.

Artificially reducing rates only makes the situation worse.  Why?  Because it increases debt and creates situations where a larger portion of society feel that being in debt is "normal" when it actually isn't. 

So homes are not "less affordable" due to higher mortgage rates.  Instead, homes start a journey to becoming "more affordable" due to higher mortgage rates... and people are forced to get into better habits with money.

Debt is still the great destroyer that it has always been.  But it has really gotten a lot worse in recent decades.  Home costs are easily triple what they should be due to our infatuation with debt-based financing.  Yes, 3x.  2x from price inflation cuased by what people feel (forgetting the duration) they can pay monthly, and another +1x from all the interest.

-Matt

My father died by suicide at age 83. He was a retired scientist and medical researcher and he had near end-stage emphysema. He knew what his future held and lived in deathly fear of the bronchial spasms which caused him severe distress, anxiety, and inability to breathe.
We knew what was coming but decided to do nothing. Dad was very clinical in his beliefs, as most scientists are, and believed that life was life and then you died. The reality is there is nothing we could have done for him that would ease his pain, and would in fact have increased his suffering.. 
When he did the deed, we grieved and mourned as would any survivor but understood it was what he wanted. He had our love and affection, and my sister and I had great childhoods. 
It was extremely difficult to explain to others what happened. I told a few of his closest friends and a few relatives but mostly kept quiet when people asked, saying he passed from complications of his emphysema. Suicide is not an easy subject to discuss. There was a obituary, but no service. A year or so later we spread his ashes in the same place as my mother's six years earlier.
I still struggle with his death 17 years later.

I feel I have some perspective to add as I have seen both sides of the AI in medicine education divide. I am a senior resident, and attended medical school from 2020-2024. I am utilizing AI tools in my medical practice and training now, but also completed much of my training prior to these tools being available. A couple points to add:

1. Medical trainees have to absorb and master much more information now than previously, and the pace is only accelerating. To give an example from oncology, the FDA has approved nearly 600 new medications for cancers alone between the time Dr. Bedard finished medical school and now. I agree the fundamentals need to be memorized and mastered to be a good physician, but the raw volume of content is a different beast now. 
2. Nearly all medical students and trainees I have encountered are extremely motivated and dedicated individuals. Despite all of the negative energy in society directed towards doctors and the healthcare system today, they chose this path anyway. Give them some grace as they navigate new technologies. Who else than the younger generations to champion incorporating new tools for the coming decades of medicine.
3. Medical training is still FULL of written exams. Nearly every week of medical school. 3 separate day long licensing exams. Specialty board exams. AI won't help students there. We are still expected and required to pass, and students know this. 

In sum, I see less cause for pessimism than you describe here.

Like other uses of AI, I want my doctor to use AI as a first step to help with efficiency. Then I want my doctor to filter AI results through his/her professional judgement.

comments.body:
We need to reckon with what we are creating: an alien intelligence in its infancy—one that is growing, learning, and improving at a pace biological evolution never prepared us to confront.
This is not merely an exceptionally powerful tool. It is the beginning of a new kind of intelligence: one that can increasingly learn from its own outputs, adapt to new problems, and operate in ways humans may not fully understand or anticipate.
If its capabilities continue to compound, the central question will no longer be whether it is smarter than us, but whether its goals remain compatible with human survival and flourishing. An intelligence millions of times more capable than humanity would not be something we could reliably control through improvisation, good intentions, or optimism.
We do not yet know how such an intelligence would behave. That uncertainty is precisely why alignment, transparency, and safeguards cannot be afterthoughts. We should not merely hope benevolence is built into the machine. We should make proving it our highest priority.

comments.name: Archibald
comments.body:
What people around the world are experiencing is what I refer to as “Screaming Monkeys Syndrome”.
When faced with any change in their environment that could be threatening, our primate cousins all start screaming at once, even if there is no real threat.
We humans do the same; our primate reflexes are still intact.
We have seen this before: the “satanic mills” of the Industrial Revolution, the development of nuclear weapons and power plants, the growth of digital computing, the “War on Drugs”, violent computer games, Y2K, - all predicted to cause the downfall of society, if not the end of the world as we’ve known it.
And now A.I. and the prophets of doom have us all screaming again.
A.I. Is clearly a powerful technological leap and undoubtedly requires oversight and regulation on an international scale, but to immediately assume it’s an existential threat is merely screaming from the trees.
A.I. Is not a “thing”, it’s ultimately a large number of variations on computer codes that can generate text and images and summarize and make predictions from massive databases.
It is, as well, already ubiquitous. A.I. coding is already integrated into institutional, government, military, economic, and social services worldwide. It is not a “thing” that can be “stopped”.
So let’s all stop screaming and deal with it rationally.
The world is not ending.

comments.name: Gowan McAvity
comments.body: The problem with apocalyptic thinking is the all or nothing mindset, but the rapture never occurs, the complete destruction of humanity and the Earth. Even asteroids and nuclear exchange would simply kill a lot of currently living creatures, perhaps most, but in geologic, and usually shortsighted human memory, everything doesn’t end, it just changes, in a very cyclical way. Sometimes in catastrophic ways. That can be mitigated though never avoided entirely. Humans are warming the biome quickly enough to imbalance systems and cause a lot of suffering in environmental catastrophe. Every living creature was destined to die anyway. This isn’t apocalyptic thinking. It is simply the way it is. Humans are ruining it for themselves and all now living. That’s not the apocalypse. We want our time to be the most significant, so many declare the apocalypse is upon us. No one really understands what that is and how many have declared it before in hopes their time has real meaning. It doesn’t. The apocalypse is a myth. Get over it. Evolution simply shrugs and moves on.

comments.name: Howard Fairman
comments.body: Why do we accept apocalyptic pronouncements as facts? We know the methodology: public debate. And we know the logical fallacy: taking a conclusion for granted in the premises (petitio principii). But these omissions are what makes news and (at least brief) fame — until the news cycle moves inexorably on.

comments.name: ialbrighton
comments.body: If the world is ending there's so many people who are saying, finally.  We can all stop pretending we like our kids or I can finally tell my boss I've imagined poisoning his dog everytime he brings it up in meetings.  And oh my god, no more meetings!  I don't have to pretend I'm excited to finally go over that spreadsheet in a zoom conference.  Or can you imagine never having to hear another where I was on 9/11 story.  Think of the plumbers who will never have to explain that it takes awhile for the tank to fill up after you flush it.  And can you imagine the relief to the people in nursing homes.  Miss Betty good news, you'll never have to pretend to your family that playing bingo once a week makes up for being confined with a bunch of people who are incontinent.  And think of all the people who will never have to hear someone ramble on about a podcast they heard.  There's so many people who would benefit from the world ending.  Can you imagine never having to hear another sports commentator say the game will come down to quarterback play.  And no more demonstrations of how to put on an oxygen mask.  We can all stop pretending we like horses or pugs.  Can you imagine never hearing someone explain exactly how drunk they were by saying we were so drunk, man.  No more Danielle Steele novels.  And no more people who think they're heroes for liking Apple products.  No more laundry.  Please, AI lords, kill us all.

comments.name: Federalist
comments.body: I read the scientific literature on global warming and look at the data and data analysis regularly. There is no question we are already passing the first tipping points that scientists like Johan Rockstrom name as Planetary Boundaries. The Earth is known by climate scientists to be on track to warm enough to trigger self accelerating interacting positive feed backs. That is why they are so strongly warning we need to rapidly cut use and production of fossil fuels. NOT keep increasing production. That the author of this article who should know better minimizes and denies this is shocking to me. I did not expect denialism from this author.

articles.title: The Problem With Apocalyptic Thinking
articles.summary: From climate to Covid to A.I., we face a terrifying feeling of exponential growth spinning out of our control. Are we right?

comments.name: SMB
comments.body:
This is Europe's fundamental problem: indecision and hand-wringing

As long as they cannot agree what to order for lunch they will continue to be pushed around by Putin and Trump.

comments.name: Ella
comments.body:
I just read about an Estonian man who was deported to Siberia with his parents during the Russian occupation. His father was shot. His mother died of starvation. He was "adopted" through a Russian orphanage — his name and birth date changed, given a Russian name, and he forgot who he was. He found out in his early fifties that he was actually Estonian, that his father had been a policeman during Estonia's independence, and that this was why both parents had been deported.

In case anyone was wondering, this is Russki Mir. The same thing is being done to Ukrainian children right now — the ICC has already issued arrest warrants for Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova specifically over it. It is not a new method. It is an old one, applied again.

I have nothing more to add.

In case anyone wants to know more, YouTube is full of videos about real life in places like Norilsk. A bus journey in minus 40°C, all the windows smashed, snow blizzard blowing through the inside.

I also recommend three books: Marquis de Custine, *Letters from Russia*. Catherine Merridale, *The Red Fortress*. And Catherine Belton, *Putin's People*.

Thankfully, Finland and Sweden have joined NATO, entirely ‘thanks’ to Mr. Putin starting this war.

comments.name: KG
comments.body: One of the things that need to be done as soon as possible, is the massive and multimodal cyberattack on ruSSia. This shall render useless their cyber capabilities to harm us and would cripple their economy. They should be immediately cut off from any and all electronic banking systems. Finally they should be cut off from the Internet backbone as soon as the cyber offensive is executed. On top of that all people holding ruSSian passports shall be banned from entering our countries.

comments.name: Sean
comments.body: Trump should recuse himself from all decisions regarding Russia. The Trump family is already compromised. They have accepted dirty Russian money to the tune of $200k from a Russian oligarch they have known for less than a year. Because they are compromised in this manner they have an actual conflict of interest. Trump can’t serve two masters simultaneously: 1) the USA and 2) the enemy of the USA, Russia. He needs to step down in order to let an unbiased, unconflicted, pro-USA party take over all issues concerning Russia.

comments.name: mike lermontov
comments.body: NATO has been involved in this war from the beginning and has already put every weapon it has into this conflict.  Still the war goes on.  More weapons for Ukraine is not going to lead to a victory over Russia.  What Ukraine really needs is soldiers and that is something that NATO does not have in significant numbers and will not commit in any event.  There is no way that the comfortable people of Western Europe are going to tolerate thousands of their young men killed on the battlefields of Ukraine.    NATO will continue to supply weapons to Ukraine and continue to excoriate Russia in the harshest terms but the desired victory in Ukraine will ever remain elusive.

comments.name: Cris
comments.body: Where I live in Spain it is full of wealthy Russians. We even have a Russian Orthodox Church here. Sometimes I think that I would be thrilled to see them all clear out, although most have residence permission. Then I remember the nice, normal Russian couple who lives on my street with their two small children, and I am determined that all of this cannot turn me into someone I no longer recognize.

comments.name: Lex
comments.body: The only language putin understands is force. Swift and brutal retaliation, aggressive escalation that russia doesn't expect and puts them on the back foot.

comments.name: Eleanor
comments.body: Provocations exist on all sides in this war. Ukraine revels in assassinations and drone attacks applauded by the West. The USA news reported that Russia attacked a train in Poland which we now understand occurred in Ukraine near the Polish border.  Denmark, Germany, Poland, UK. France, Lithuania, and along with other European nations provide arms, surveillance,  and funds without accountability. And of course, the USA provides surveillance capability to Ukraine and sells arms to Europe to be used in Ukraine again without accountability. Europe, which gambled on easily defeating Russia, is now suffering economically as ordinary folks are bearing the costs of this war.  Very worrisome is the rise of the Right in Germany and its re-militarization. Germany has not forgotten that the Soviet Union contributed to its defeat in WWII. If we want WWIII, we are headed in that direction with the possibility of nukes being employed. It is time to find a peaceful solution to this war which, along with our involvement in Iran and Palestine, is impoverishing ordinary folks in the USA, not to forget causing the loss of so many lives in Ukraine and Russia. We need to stop cheering for WWIII and focus on compromise and war ending solutions.

Democrats don’t trust elections because it’s painfully obvious that Trump and his Republican minions will, in fact, steal elections.

It is up to us white people to vote in massive numbers to put an end to this corrupt regime.

comments.name: James DeRohan
comments.body: It is easy to dismiss press access when officials respond to reasonable questions with evasion, hostility or outright nonsense. But that misses the point. The value of a free press does not depend on those in power being candid, courteous or even willing to answer. It depends on journalists retaining the right to be there, to ask the question, to press for an answer and to place the response — or the refusal to respond — on the public record. Democracy is weakened not only when the truth is suppressed, but when the opportunity to demand it is allowed to disappear.

comments.name: kad
comments.body: Its all personal point of view, when one does not want to see truth. If you're a fan of the man, you're on his side on this issue. If you're hardcore "on the other side", doesn't matter what he does—you'll hate it. With this issue, I view whats happening as reported: attempting to control all narratives, no dissent, no criticisms or takedowns allowed. Ultimately I'm really hoping no future leader will attempt to do the things he's done. If that happens, we are in even more trouble going forward.

comments.name: RjW

I want to propose the following:
Continue the united press front.
Report audio and written reports, and show no video. 
He loves seeing his mug on TV. His voice and commentary will keep us all informed of his lies and deceit. 
When he starts calling reporters fake, nasty, etc., they all should turn their backs and/or walk away.

We apparently cannot punish Trump himself. 
So let's make it legally dangerous to work for him. 
This order to ban the press from the White House was enacted by someone. In fact there's certainly a chain of "someones" who heard Trump's obviously illegal order and enforced it. Sue every one of them. Take them out of their jobs and force them to hire lawyers and spend their time defending themselves in court. I cannot imagine an excuse for carrying out an obviously illegal order. We all know there's a First Amendment, right?

If Chief Justice Roberts has any patriotism left in him, he should get out in front of this and directly tell Trump that SCOTUS will reject all false allegations of election fraud.

comments.body: State TV anyone? Trump was stopped in this attempt to completely control the narrative and suppress our free press, but if his attempts to undermine the judiciary were to go through as he hopes, then all bets are off.

comments.name: OD
comments.body:
As public Trump regime defiance of a court order draws ever nearer, Americans need to worry about the US Marshals Service. 

Would they enforce a contempt order against Trump or his cabinet ministers? All US "law enforcement" is suffused with Trumpism and authoritarianism, and the Marshals are certainly no exception to that. 

The US National Judges Association meeting last year discussed setting up a new security service that would be controlled and paid by the judiciary, not the executive. It's obvious they share my fears. 

When that meeting was reported, and the USMS was asked for comment, they huffily responded that "of course US Marshals will always protect judges."

But that wasn't the question. The question is whether US Marshals will enforce judges' orders against powerful Republicans, as their duty demands. And the Marshals had nothing to say on that.

comments.name: Zen master PDX
comments.body:
As a South Asian American and a Muslim who was born in India, I find the most troubling part of this story to be the suggestion that an entire community is foreign or suspect. Americans can disagree about immigration policy. But judging Sikh truck drivers, students, physicians, or business owners by their appearance, religion, or surname is discrimination, not a policy argument.

We also need to confront prejudice within our own communities. Muslims, Christians, and other religious minorities in India deserve the same solidarity we seek for South Asians facing hostility in America. That principle was brought into sharp focus when Mohan Bhagwat, the head of India’s RSS, was welcomed at a large event organized by Hindu American groups in New York. Many Indian Americans supported the event; others opposed it because of concerns about the RSS’s treatment of religious minorities. We cannot demand inclusion here while overlooking exclusion that affects others.

Words from elected officials and government agencies carry particular weight. They can make prejudice seem acceptable, regardless of intent. No one should have to prove they are “really American” because their name is Singh, Patel, or Desai. Citizenship and shared values matter more than ancestry.

Our opposition to racism, xenophobia, and religious intolerance must be consistent, whoever the target may be.

comments.name: MR
comments.body: I am Indian American and have always opposed Trump precisely because the writing was always on the wall. Now the chickens have come home to roost. I hope this is a wake up call to all the Indian Americans who supported Trump for selfish reasons like lower taxes and a booming stock market. I hope many of them will now choose to vote blue so we can reverse this blind hate and bigotry.

comments.name: Matthew Carnicelli
comments.body:
The truth is that Trump has given many Americans the permission to allow their most primitive and antisocial impulses to rise to the surface.  

No one should ever confuse Trump with a proper role model - not in business, not in politics, and certainly not in life.  

Trump's encouragement of nativist groups has been especially toxic, and is now even negatively impacting voters who supported him.

Hate is not a solution to any of our problems.  If Americans want a greater nation, then they need to become more savvy voters.

Don't blame the immigrant doing their best to achieve the American dream.  Blame the politicians, like Trump, who have rigged the game so that only the corrupt fat cats truly win.

comments.name: Sir Sidney Ruff-Diamond
comments.body:
As a first-generation South Asian immigrant raised in a Hindu family, I deeply value the cultural diversity that immigrants bring to this nation. However, I am opposed to the construction of massive temples and statues, which I view as a wasteful use of resources. Having moved to America in search of peace and quiet, I dislike the public display of religion, loud religious music, and large processions reminiscent of the environment back in India. While most Americans are decent and respectful enough to tolerate these disruptions, we should not take advantage of their goodwill.
This need for restraint feels even more urgent today. Since Prime Minister Modi came to power, India has increasingly become a hostile environment for religious minorities like Muslims and Christians. Witnessing this climate fuel a growing wave of Hindu nationalism right here among Indian Americans is deeply concerning and disappointing.

comments.name: Ciudad Galveston
comments.body: I live in Texas and French’s remarks made headlines statewide. Coincidentally, my next door neighbors are Indian. He’s a retired engineer and they’ve been transferred all over the globe. It is one of those super high-achieving families. Their daughter was valedictorian of her class at the university and then the London School of Economics. Best neighbors we’ve ever had.

comments.name: Vin
comments.body: When I was growing up, we'd look back on the era when open racism was acceptable in this country as backwards and shameful. Fifty years hence, future generations will be looking upon our time in the same way.

comments.name: ShipHasSailed
comments.body: To echo (in a different way) what some other commenters have said:  when bad policies and disparaging/racist rhetoric is directed to “others”, everyone else just acts like an unaffected bystander.  But then, after some time, those bystanders become the “other”, and then they realize that our problems here are deeply ingrained and systemic.  They will unfortunately find that sooner or later, depending on the whims of their fellow countrymen and the political winds pushing their leaders, the tide will turn against them, when they least expect it, and through no fault of their own.  Many of these individuals said they voted for Trump multiple times, because they thought that only the “others” would be affected.  Now they see that anyone can be caught in the crosshairs of hatred.  Lesson learned?

comments.name: Chris LaCass
comments.body: It's sad that Sikhs are being targeted on US soil by followers of both Trump and Modi. It seems nationalism and hatred have no borders and evil thrives because good men haven't learned the lessons of history. It's an election year and, historically 50% of registered voters fail to vote in midterm elections. Perhaps the best thing each one of us can do is to get everyone we know to vote in November. That could make a difference.

comments.name: GCA
comments.body: The US has had limited leverage with China for quite some time, and Trump has been voluntarily ceding pretty much everything we still had. Our superior higher education system, our lagging but at least competitive position on renewable energy production, what turns out to be an illusion about our military's absolute superiority, the strength of our close relationship with allies... I could go on. Trump is driving the nation into the ditch, and Xi knows it. Why would he possibly give up anything to Trump when he holds all the cards and he knows it.

comments.name: Deckard
comments.body:
I'm sorry, the self-proclaimed “Greatest Nation” is struggling with China’s industrial output? 

Please, the USA lost that edge decades ago. 

China’s industrial technology output is beyond the reach of not just the U.S., but the entire industrialized world; it lost that edge, and it will never catch up.   

The only genuine export the U.S.A. has is its branded hypocrisy of DemocraZy, where the motto is, Do as we tell you; don't do as we do.

China continues to invest in its future, from infrastructure to technology, education, health care, housing, a multi-pronged energy approach, and so much more.

China's continued path toward energy self-reliance, along with its vast crude reserves, gives it unmatched leverage.

I strongly recommend that everyone start learning Mandarin. 

Ni Hao Ma.

comments.name: apparatchik
comments.body: There are collateral consequences to Trump's buddying up to Xi.  It's clear Trump is schmoozing Xi, trying to impress him and show the world how well his personal charm and toughness can influence events.  All the while, Xi is observing close up how much Trump has declined, mentally and physically.  Showing up at Andrews wearing an overcoat and gloves was a huge mistake.  For a guy who prizes image, he whiffed on that one.

comments.name: Dan O
comments.body:
Call me silly, but before I would upset an important provider of items your country uses, I'd get my ducks in a row and try to find other providers to see what benefits there would be for larger purchases, etc. If you do your homework you might have a stronger negotiation outcome with that biggest provider. 

Trump does it a little differently. He likes to upset everyone to see what shakes, including the provider's you might really need in tough times. Right now that strategy is creating higher prices for everything, including gas, and, for the cherry on top, higher interest rates for home mortgages. 

And, it's supported by the GOP Congress!!!

Don't forget to vote in the midterm elections!!!

comments.name: Two Cents
comments.body:
It’s just embarrassing that we have such a weak-minded president who represents sloppiness in thought, action and planning. 

In line with Trump’s struggles to find leverage with Xi, most of the imagery from this gathering shows a contrast between Xi, who seems to carry himself with the demeanor of a statesman, and Trump, who seems like nothing but vapid bluster and garishness, sometimes giving a sloppy military salute. 

In the way they dress, Xi’s suit seems simple, formal and tailored. Trump is wearing a long coat that generally hasn’t been in style for about two decades. His suits often don’t fit him properly. As big as he seems, his suits look frumpy and too big for him. No comment on his hair. 

In every picture I’ve seen, they also do not seem happy to be together. Trump often has a frown or a scowl. Xi has a neutral look or smile as if thinking this can’t be over soon enough

Finally, anyone who’s seen a top notch marching band can see that those soldiers lining the red carpet also look sloppy. Their feet aren’t aligned; they’re holding the rifles at different heights and at slightly different angles; the placement of their hands on the rifles isn’t uniform. Everything should be perfectly aligned, especially for a ceremonious occasion like this one.

Think Xi didn’t notice? Watch any footage of the Chinese military with Xi riding before them. EVERYTHING is perfectly aligned, even their heads as they seem to group soldiers by height.

comments.name: Shine Awake
comments.body: The United States encouraged China to join the World Trade Organization therefore improving China's economic standing, strength and power in the world. That way, US companies could profit from cheap labor and lack of human rights and regulations protecting the environment. It was a strategic mistake. China has played the game well. If I was betting, I would bet on Xi.

comments.name: Keith wheelock
comments.body:
As a former Foreign Service Officer with boots on the ground in Asia, I am amused that Trump is speaking of himself and President Xi as ‘G2’—the two top leaders in the world.

The Japanese word for status is ‘kan’. Over the past year Xi’s global kan has soared, while Trump’s kan has plummeted. Xi must be bemused by watching Trump lose more and more global kan while China has surpassed the United States.

I feel that Trump is playing poker with a pair of deuces. My fear is that he will ignorantly stumble into big blunders while XI smilingly gives the Atlanta zoo two pandas and invites 100,000 US students to China.

I especially fear how Trump has greatly weakened America’s military commitment in Asia, while Xi is slithering towards Taiwan.

comments.name: EJS
comments.body: Waiting forTrump to play hardball with China and raise tariffs on them.  Then sitting back to see how long it takes China to cancel rare Earth metal shipments to the US.  Then watch as Trump completely backtracks and somehow calls it 'winning'.   China has put engineers in its leadership roles.  The US has put Poly-sci majors, lawyers and Fox News hosts in charge.  Lesson for US - the pain is only going to magnify for some time.  What will be left of our country is hard to say/

comments.name: Kevin Kostyk

comments.name: David A.

comments.name: Cindy Dore
comments.body: I worked for hospitals for many years. They always upcoded to charge insurance companies more. Total ripoff.  Now AI is assisting them to defraud the consumer even more. Infuriating!

comments.name: J M
comments.body: Broken vertebrae three years ago, CT denied as not medically necessary as was the kyphoplasty.  Certain blood tests denied for PV, a blood cancer (2023), as not medically necessary but I did have the disease.  The former CT and surgery denial was reversed on peer review.  The blood tests were not ever reversed but once I was positive with JAK2, somehow I was not billed.  My husbands stage 4a prostate cancer surgery payment was denied, that after sending us a pre-approval (2024).  We have Medicare PPO Advantage costing $525 a month each.  We are not well off but need this coverage.  Your article was not encouraging.

comments.name: claudia
comments.body:
Neurologist in the Bronx
Yesterday I called a primary care doctor' s office at a prestigious facility to get a HIP referral (HIP of New York is one of the few insurances requiring a HIP generated referral to see a specialist)
I had my first encounter with an AI agent (Marie)> after exchanging unnecessary pleasantries Marie asked how she could help. I said: HIP referral. Answer: right or left?
pretty pathetic

comments.name: Dan Smith
comments.body:
Health care in America is so despicable. It's trendy to blame the insurers but it's the doctors and practices as well. The bottom line is everything.

I will never in my life forget sitting in the Orthopedist's office the morning after a major sports injury. Requiring surgery to correct. I asked something to the effect of "am I likely to reinjure it if I fall or something while it's healing? And what is likely to happen?" Doc let out a gleeful laugh and proudly said "well then I get paid to fix it again."

Super.

There are literally people whose full-time job is to churn cards and earn equivalent yearly wages higher than US income median. I personally manage 40+ credit cards for my household and 10+ of them have annual fee around $700-900, but i actually have net gains from them each year without actual travel or fine-dining. It's not always about "show off" or "Gen Z privileges", just pure economics and math. The costs of medical care are twice as high in this country because of high overhead costs and redundant services rather than price gouging by caregivers. Markets tend to exacerbate that problems with uncertainties resulting from the risks differing between pools of people covered. The solutions are very hard to fix, as physicians who study the economics of the system soon appreciate. 

Medicare for all seems to be a simple fix but it’s just no fix at all. The patients served will not resemble those served by Medicare and the neither will the providers. There will need to be big changes to how ailments are recorded and measured to determine the risks which anticipate costs and the funds to cover them. The services provided need to be known to reduce redundant care which requires having a common source of knowing who got what and when. Compensation for care must be standardized. Just enrolling all in Medicare would overnight disrupt care fur all indefinitely.

This is an excellent interview and does help to ease some of my anxiety about Abdul El Sayed.  While I do hope that he wins - the need to end Republican control of the Senate outweighs everything else - I don't really trust him.  But there is more nuance here than I expected:  I particularly appreciate his acknowledgement of Jewish trauma and the right of Jewish Israelis to self-determination.
But, sadly, he is still struggling against the image that he chose to present of himself in the primary. As a frequent contributor to Democratic candidates, I received numerous fundraising requests from him daily, via FB and email. They all had the same message: The most critical priority in the Senatorial race was the defeat of not MAGA but AIPAC.  Even when another issue, like healthcare, was mentioned, AIPAC was identified as the enemy; i.e. we don't have national healthcare because AIPAC has ensured that every spare penny in the budget goes to Israel.
To be clear, I don't agree with or give money to AIPAC. But the notion that AIPAC - which is only #18 on Open Secrets's list of large political donor organizations, well behind Space-X and several crypto companies - is somehow the prime mover behind everything that is wrong with our country, is ridiculous -sort of the left-wing version of the right wing's "Synagogue of Satan."

This scrutiny demonstrated in hindsight that Trump had effectively, if tacitly, endorsed these people and their ideas. The savvy media consumer was thus put on guard against subsequent silent elevations of white supremacy and white protestant ethno-nationalism.

El-Sayed has an analogous problem, bigly, but he got a free pass from Klein.

It's also fair for voters to judge El-Sayed by the company he keeps, and let me say it from my chest, El-Sayed kept company with Piker, knowing full well who he was and what he believed. articles.title: His Debut Novel Was a Literary Sensation. Was It Actually Written by AI?
articles.summary: The author of “C’était ça ou Mourir” (“It Was Either That or Die”) has defended his writing style in the face of accusations that he wrote the book using artificial intelligence.

comments.name: DAVID BENSON

comments.body: The situation reflects as badly on the literary critics and. contest judges as on anyone else. No taste, judgement or qualifications from either group.

comments.name: Tiger Reve
comments.body:
Before you comment, try a simple experiment. Write three paragraphs about something ordinary: what you made for dinner last night, your drive or train ride to work this morning, or any mundane moment from your day. Then paste them into Pangram. There’s a free version. When I tried this, about 80% of my own writing was flagged as AI-generated or AI-assisted.

Pangram says it trains its detector on human writing and AI-written imitations, and claims a very low false positive rate. It still got my writing wrong. Try it yourself and see what you get.

Pangram did not observe my writing process. It made a prediction based on the text, and that prediction was wrong. Its label alone is not proof of how I wrote the passage.

I expect lawsuits as people challenge false accusations based on these results.

comments.name: BOB SCHAFER
comments.body: Isn’t AI a writing style?

comments.name: Patricia Sette
comments.body:
What bothers me about this is how ready we are to convict this man on the basis of AI detection "evidence," which, in fact, is not evidence.  Most people happily "piling on" here would have no idea what the percentage in these AI verdicts means, unless they run off and search now for what it means. . (There are basically two meanings, which can vary with the kind of detector.) 

If this were a crime, and Claudel could go to prison, could any conscientious juror say there was real "evidence" to convict? No, because there is no real "evidence," just suggestion. Yet we are willing to convict him in the court of public opinion, even at the risk of being wrong, and ruin his future. It is a deep wrong to harm someone's reputation when you're not sure he deserves it.

comments.body: So the prompts are the actual intellectual property that belongs to the author???

comments.name: CHARLES WHITE
comments.body:
Just for fun, I inserted a Claude-written graf into an essay-in-progress and ran it through an AI detector. Its response: "This is an excellent, original paragraph" blah, blah, blah. I then ran an original graf through the app. Its response: "This seems to be an AI-generated paragraph." 

The detectors are not yet accurate, and we're already getting our knickers in a twist. Let's face it. There are acceptable degrees of AI use for writers:  extraordinary access to research, specific citations, edits, tracking continuity, generating ideas, etc.  

Accurately identifying writers' use of AI is going to be a slog. The heads of both the guilty and the innocent will roll. Let's not be Luddites and toss the baby out with the bathwater.

/mrs.

Hard to conceive of someone asserting that executing 18 year olds must be prohibited but that the penalty is acceptable for a 19 or 22 year old. In any case, the only real argumentation here concerns the intense abuse the murderer had endured prior to committing the crime.  That is a fundamentally different issue than a flat age limit for the death penalty. If she had been 21, suddenly the abuse is irrelevant?  This article is all over the place, and its approach can only confirm the views of death penalty abolitionists while failing to convince any death penalty proponent that 18 year olds should always be spared the penalty. Not clear if the latter argument is even made here, since it seems that having been severely abused is another necessary criterion of the author here to oppose the penalty in this particular case. To make the ‘age limit’ argument, consider a case where the perpetrator had never been abused at all, but simply enjoyed committing torture and murder.

comments.name: Jonesy
comments.body:
When I was a graduate student in American history decades ago, I worked as an assistant to a professor who specialized in the post-Civil War south--not my field; I was a Colonialist. One assignment was to tabulate lynchings across the south by county between the end of Reconstruction and 1910, using data originally compiled by Ida B. Wells and then continued and published by the NAACP. Talk about a depressing! 

Coming from a white family deeply rooted in the south and somewhat involved in "the movement," I  knew some of this, vaguely, but the accumulation of detail taught me a lot. The first thing was how much variation there was when it came to "lynching." It has never simply been a matter hanging someone by a rope from a tree. Ask any of the families killed by being trapped in cabins set afire by night riders. But the main surprise was how many white people were lynched. Counting white deaths wasn't part of my assignment, and it took me a while to notice the trend, but I had expected virtually NO white victims, but the enumerators registered far more than that. My mental estimate came to as many as 25 to 30 percent of the total. I was stunned. What was going on? I can't say for sure but two things immediately come to mind: people caught up in the emptying of jails, and politics. It's now well accepted that many of the people targeted for lynching were labor organizers, particularly working to organizer farm workers and sharecroppers, and a lot of those folks were white.

Israel’s subsequent targeted self-defense operations in a dense urban battlefield where the enemy operates from civilian areas was not genocide.

comments.name: David Fieldman

Trump Xi Jinping Pageantry Plus,  2026

Picture the scene: red carpets rolled out, military brass bands blaring, and fighter jets soaring overhead in a display of grand American pomp—all to honor Xi Jinping over a lavish state dinner. Meanwhile, Beijing is quietly bankrolling and strategically bolstering Iran, the very nation Donald Trump is currently threatening with total annihilation from the podium at the United Nations. It is a masterclass in cognitive dissonance: raising a glass of vintage Cabernet to the patron saint of the government you’re actively threatening to turn into ash.

But the surrealism doesn't stop at global proxy conflicts. The real irony peaks when the cameras start rolling. Chinese state media journalists—accustomed to rigid state control and heavily censored press pools at home—are granted VIP, unfettered access to capture every smile, handshake, and toast. Meanwhile, American outlets like CNN, Politico, and MSNOW find themselves barred at the door, exiled from covering their own president in his own house.

In this inverted reality, a foreign authoritarian state’s media apparatus gets the front-row seat to democracy's spectacle, while domestic journalists are treated like uninvited crashers. 

It’s a pure diplomatic farce: roll out the red carpet for your chief adversary's ally, hand their press corps the microphone, and lock your own reporters in the hallway. 

Bizarre doesn't even begin to cover it.

comments.name: TG
comments.body:
A very informative, wide-ranging, empathetic article. As a 74-year-old classical pianist who's dealt with a mild case of something called focal dystonia (briefly, a malfunctioning of the fine motor system) for over 20 years now, I can attest to the reluctance of classical musicians to talk about any problems they think might hurt them career-wise. 
This reluctance is fortunately now giving way to more opennness, and therefore often to real progress in treating and dealing with the various issues that beset musicians.
Being a classical musician is really hard work, literally hands-on work. It consumes us, demands the utmost of us, every day. But this physical act is guided by our psyches, our intelligence, our hearts, our personal identification with the work and the results. We feel like our lives are at stake!
And it doesn't get any easier as we get older, let alone if we're well-known and have a public reputation on the line every time we go out on stage. Many legendary soloists have had to be virtually pushed out onto the stage - sometimes not without throwing up backstage first. 
I applaud Ms. Koh for her candor in talking about her journey, and I thank Mr. Barone for describing it. I might add that whatever the external results of this journey, it's always also an invitation - from ourselves to ourselves - that cannot be declined, an invitation to engage in a process that inevitably leads us deeper into ourselves and the act of making music.

That’s a critical it misses.

comments.name: murdoch
comments.body: Computer assisted DNA and RNA sequence similarity searches have been around for years and lots of reverse transcriptase genes and gene fragments have been found. That a fancier computer program found a few more is a yawn. The real work behind this was all the isolation and sequencing from animals, bacteria and viruses by scientists all around the world and the cooperative assembly of data bases; the type of international scientific cooperation that the current administration is fighting against. The real news in this announcement is why does Anthropic think it needs to make a Major Biology Discovery announcement; probably just an internal political move from a corporate subdivision to increase its share of Anthropics budget.

Every time I am brought back to remembering my five years living within the Lake Elsinore city limits, I reminisce over the story of how its name originated. I was friends with the son of a migrants family whose relatives were instrumental in the process. Apparently, this family found that San Diego wasn’t suitable enough for them to settle down and continued to migrate inland following the trek now known as I-15.  
Approximately 50 miles north they’d happened upon the large lake that now bears the name of the city and relocated permanently on its shore as it was teeming with many species of fish. Unfortunately, much of the life in the lake died off over the summer and the stench of rotting fish permeated the atmosphere surrounding the city for miles. 

It was during a job interview with a well known and prosperous family from the area that had asked how his family was enjoying their new home from where they’d immigrated from Mexico, and without missing a beat he’d replied, “is like Hell, señor!”  

There was never a truer statement ever opined.

It was ultimately a dead-end and he couldn’t overcome his limitations as both an artist and a deeply flawed person. Krasner grew and evolved in form, color, range and complexity. For me Lee and Joan Mitchell(!) are the two leading lights from whom I get the most to look at and live in, the most poetry and music and human feeling, the most mature and universe and possibility of thought. comments.body: A great article.  I so relate to it.  I was a newly graduated painter who met this guy who made marbled works as a career for many years.  He carried himself well, had a lot of creative energy and got noticed.  I quickly learned the technique and brought my exceptional talents to the practice.  We thrived in the marketplace until his violent, dark side became a publicly hidden but huge impediment both to our livelihood and my safety.  I divorced him under intensely difficult circumstances.  A couple of years later, I came across a Facebook chat among fellow artisan guys we both knew, discussing him. In passing I was mentioned, as the "wife" who may be out of the picture.  Stunning, absolutely stunning!  In an instance, I lost all respect for them.  One of the prominent speakers "has a wife" who is a well known, successful artisan in her field.  To this day I wonder if she knows who her husband is.  The frail egos and male chauvinism runs deep. Very deep.  It explains everything we encounter in any professional field.  A contemporary woman painter I admire is Cecily Brown.  She seems to embody a woman feeling free to be true to herself.  If you saw her paintings without knowing the artist, would it be "woman's work"?  I believe emphasizing artists' gender is derogatory and certainly divisive beyond doubt.

Krasner is one of the few NY based female abstract expressionists that already has extensive museum representation and market validation with prices for her work at auction eclipsing $10 million. Agreed that this benchmark lands well below work by Pollack but  the price for her work is now very much more than any mere mortal can afford. Now that Krasner and the small NY school of female abstract expressionists(many schooled by Hans Hofmann) have been rediscovered, I suggest that it is long past time to rediscover the legion of talented midcentury artists of both genders and give them their due recognition for the contributions that they have made by giving them an exhibition of their own.

Frankly, I don’t doubt that AI can do good; it obviously can. AI saves time, and time is one of the primary constraints on what we do. I suspect many people do less research than they ought because they simply don’t have enough time and still have deadlines to meet.

AI can be a good starting point for research. Before AI, it was common to spend hours or days sifting through articles and cases, hoping to find something that sounded like it might be saying something useful. AI can cut down the “find something that sounds like it might be interesting” part considerably. You still have to read and evaluate the sources, but that alone saves a great deal of time and makes thorough research much more compatible with real-world deadlines. Time is money, and if AI can reduce the time required for research, it may also make lower-cost medical or legal services more feasible.

But at the same time, when I look back on the past three years of working with AI, I notice how close I came at times to making serious errors. I still sometimes spend hours working through problems with AI, though much less frequently than I used to.

I think AI is a tool, and I think it can do a great deal of good with proper boundaries. I just also think it is a difficult tool to use well. So it worries me because I think it will spread far and wide. I don't think you can stop people from using it, given its obvious utility. I really do think we need widespread education on AI, but I doubt it'd happen.

My basic physics ed reminds me of a pesky thing called "Entropy,"along with "conservation of energy." Sending stuff into orbit is very costly in both the hardware and fuel; once there, the temperatures are not easily brought down, without the cheap relatively abundant water on the surface. Space is not benign; radiation and particle collisions threaten everything, including computers. Then there is the matter of transferring massive amounts of data via radio, vastly slower than modern fiber optic ground cables. Data Centers are built from myriad smaller units, and the logistics around super-fast efficient connectivity is a large hurdle, that locating in orbit makes more, not less problematic.
  Trying to massively upscale any technology butts up against entropy, which dictates that every level of organization requires more and more energy input to keep functioning, which is why these Centers are huge energy and water hogs. And one pesky feature the zealous Futurists can't explain is, what exactly is going on in them, and why do we literally see very little physical output or benefits? Idiotic AI imagery, et al, is worthless garbage. Promises of a Bright Tomorrow have been foisted since the first World's Fairs of the late 1800's, but the 1964 New York Tomorrowland has not yet given us flying cars and clean, stress-free living.

She was one of only ten people in the country who held a professional certification from ACVREP. 

The product is not studied with people with visual impairments. Meta did not sign any indemnity agreements  with the organization. The product is rife with privacy issues, and it is hard to establish informed consent when the only indicator is a tiny light that is accessible visually. On top of that,  the technology is not capable of detecting fast moving options. If someone uses this as an access tool, they could get killed. (My daughter is particularly sensitive to the prospect of someone getting hurt; a previous student was killed after allegedly pushed in front of a Miami-Dade County bus and the police never found the killer). This product is not safe to be distributed to people as an aid.

comments.name: Curtis
comments.body: "The great musicians in the Cleveland Orchestra should be compensated fairly." The financial details aren't reported here, but if revenue (and presumably, profit) is declining, then "fair" would suggest that the musicians also share in the burden.

comments.name: Here
comments.body:
How many hours do they work per week?

20 on-site service hours per week, which includes rehearsals and performances.

They are asking for a base salary of $200,000, so that's about $200 per hour minimum.

The average hourly pay for a doctor in Cleveland is about $150 per hour. Musicians are talented but they don't save lives.

Musicians will say that their "work" hours include "practice". But so does every profession, doctors, lawyers, accountants. If my doctor billed me for the hours he spent keeping up his medical skills and license, he'd not be my doctor for long.

comments.name: QTCatch10
comments.body: The AFM is up there with police unions among the most blinkered and self destructive labor organizations. Going on strike because the annual double digit percentage raises on offer arent enough (on salaries that are already generally well into six figures) is bad enough, but the contempt with which musicians often treat the staff is shameful. I'm a musician and former union member (tho not AFM) and have worked at a half dozen such organizations as a staff member and as a performer -- and I don't know what would have to happen for me to ever be on the side of the AFM. They are poisonous.

comments.name: Aziza Wahby

comments.name: Tom

comments.name: Howell
comments.body:
To all the Canadian readers who may be disgusted with America and feel that the damage is beyond repair: 

I can hardly blame you. If I were you I'm sure I'd feel the same. I'd even go so far as to say that while circumstances persist, former friends and allies have a moral duty to oppose the United States, which has become a dangerous rogue nation under Trump.

Trump will be gone in two years (at the latest) and with any luck, his Republican lackeys will lose control of Congress in November. But the MAGA crowd that gave us this deranged President isn't going away any time soon. It's a sobering thought. 

All that having been said, I will not disavow this nation that I love so well. Throughout it's history, America has aspired to and occasionally achieved true greatness, not Trump's curdled version of it. That potential remains within us, too. 

Nor will I allow myself to feel any less warmly toward our neighbors to the north, however trying the times may be. 

I sincerely hope that when this shameful chapter in our history ends, Canadians will begin to remember their kinship with the United States and understand that some of us here have never wavered in our respect and admiration for the Canadian people. 

Anger and mistrust will linger. It's been well earned. But in the end, whether we acknowledge it or not, our two nations need each other, perhaps now more than ever. Rapprochement is still possible...eventually. That's not naiveté. It's what I choose to believe.

comments.body: I know what whimsy used to be, and didn't know about this trend.  Rhinestones on cars and disposable cups??? How can something be 'whimsical' when it's copied from some source that tells you to do it?  What's creative there? When I read articles like this, it's like news of some dreadful plague that I hadn't heard of yet.  There seems to be more than enough superficiality in the world these days.

comments.name: Sid McDonough
comments.body: My wife and I sailed our ketch named Whimsy along the east coast from Maine to Florida and the Bahamas for twenty years until we aged out. We had many experiences which seemed magical including surviving bad weather. The previous owner named her and we decided to keep her name. It was perfect for two seniors setting out on the big adventure of our lives.

comments.name: Winey
comments.body:
I'm 71 years old. I will tell you what whimsy means to me. In a world of confusion and dire consequences of those idiots in power, over which I have no control but to vote, and to what avail is that? I know full well what's going on, but I refuse to allow it to rob me of what joy I can glean from this existence. Whimsy is humor, light and beauty.

It isn't ignorance or denial; it’s a conscious refusal to let the chaos outside extinguish the inner light. When the weight of the world—and the frustration of watching it be managed by people who should know better—feels overwhelming, claiming joy, humor, and beauty isn't a retreat from reality. It’s an act of defiance.

True whimsy isn't a plastic accessory you buy to pretend everything is fine. It’s the sharp, defiant spark of choosing wonder anyway. It’s finding humor in the absurd, seeking out beauty where it has no commercial purpose, and keeping your capacity for delight intact, precisely because the world seems so intent on grinding it down.

In that light, whimsy isn't childish at all. It’s a form of resilience. It says, "The world may be heavy, but it doesn't get to make me heavy."

comments.name: E
comments.body: I think people should just live their lives and do what makes them happy. If being childlike and curious is part of who you are, if you get genuinely excited about certain things, have at it! If that’s not your thing and you find all that silly, that’s ok too. Do what brings you joy and enchantment. People should look inside themselves to discover what brings them joy, not just look online for the next trend or bit of advice.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body: Whimsy is reminding me of "flair" in the film Office Space. Soon, we'll be punished by managemnet for not putting enough "whimsy" on our disposable cups!

comments.name: AnnMarie
comments.body:
As someone who strongly believes that "whimsy" is a key ingredient in making something playful, this article was fascinating to me. The phrase"Whimsymaxxing" was new to me. The entire idea of "maxxing" is something that I struggle to understand. The older I get, and the more companies/organizations I work with, the more I believe in "Enough-ing."  Striving for "as much as possible" of anything is a losing quest. We don't need everything in life to be cheaper or faster. Similarly, I believe whimsy loses its power when we try to make everything whimsical.

When designing for whimsy, the key (in my work) is "enough" and "authentic." 

So to answer the question posed by this article: "Has a dash of 'Whimsy' become less whimsical?"   I would answer... "No. A dash of whimsy is delightful, it's a bucketful of forced whimsy that loses its power."

articles.title: Has a Dash of ‘Whimsy’ Become Less Whimsical?
