comments.name: Wendy Temple
comments.body:
This happened to me, very unexpectedly. I had been single for 20 years, was pretty good by myself...and then love marched right in on the eve of my 68th birthday. A man I had known when I was much younger asked me to go with him to see a Spoleto event. A month later, I asked him over for lunch. Very platonic.

Then a few weeks later we decided to go to a movie together, and that was it! I have had an amazing life with him over the past two years that I never expected. He is brilliant, kind, and funny. He's very progressive, and an activist, which suits me to a T.

I say go for it when love walks in. We don't know what the future holds or how much time we have. I just turned 70 and he is 66.

Life is such a journey, it can surprise you.

comments.name: RonRich
comments.body:
I think politics plays a lesser role in most people's lives than appears in the media.
If I wanted someone to vote like me, think like me, buy like me, eat like me I already have that person. Me.

comments.name: Marlboro Man
comments.body:
'a Republican who doesn’t eat oysters', is this some sort of archetype? I can't blame anyone for not eating oysters, especially raw oysters. Unless you have their provenance, I would also be skeptical. Besides, oysters are these sliming gooey non descript things who filter feed in the shallows of river mouths with these rivers carrying all sorts of human refuse in their water. Do you have any idea what is in the Mississipi River? The closer the river gets to the gulf the dirtier the water as human effluent is carried to the ocean. Oysters are sucking this stuff in, filtering it, and concentrating it in their bodies. The idea of eating that is disgusting. Its all well and good that Grandma likes her oysters and her son considers anyone who doesn't eat them as undeserving of his mothers attention but maybe he will change his tune when he gets hepatitis form his oyster eating, just sayin
And the other characteristic the son finds distasteful, Republicanism. Why is this important to him. The son is biased and has drank the koolaid offered to him b the MSM. He should consider each person as who they are, not what they are labeled by preconceived notions.

comments.name: Beth
comments.body:
Jane, I absolutely loved your piece, loved the way you moved through the story. 
I hope you keep writing because you have a real talent for it.
Thank you!

comments.name: lesle acoca
comments.body: Thank you for this warm, wonderful, and hopeful mini memoir about later love.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: With age can come wisdom, but also skepticism which can bleed into cynicism. As a 67 year old who recently re-entered the dating scene after never thinking I would, I know I am the better for it. As David French said in these pages (or cyberspace) citing the Swedish proverb: “Shared joy is a double joy, shared sorrow is half a sorrow."

comments.name: Hank Linderman
comments.body:
Dating in the 70s has definitely been different, but from loneliness, to connection, to love - was just as poignant a journey as it had ever been in my past. We met through a mutual friend, and began by texting for 10 days, ultimately for hours every evening. Then days of phone calls, before meeting in person. This was a revelation - our differences would have prevented any progress if we had initially met in person.

Our relationship looks roughly like being married 2 to 4 days a week. We both have full lives, we are both set in some of our ways, full time marriage doesn't appear to be in our future. But, we are not alone anymore, life is beautiful.

And where I used to look for the closest fit in terms of social / political / religious etc. attitudes, I learned through falling in love with someone different from me the opportunities for mutual growth in crossing some dividing lines. This is a journey I wish more of us would take - learning to be willing to accept, and to be willing to give understanding, to someone with a somewhat different alignment.

Best...H

comments.name: Kevin
comments.body:
I found Vick when she was 70. I was 65. We met at a tantra group which was a great way to start. She moved out to my  remote hunting ranch and even put up with an ex I was housing.
I was recovering from a divorce after 35 year and two kids  and she was a survivor of 4 disappointing marriages. We were so different. I was a surgeon grounded in a scientifically based world view and she was a psychologist who had a collection of goddess statues and set up alters around the house and seldom saw a doctor. But we both had wide open hearts and met somewhere in the middle. It became the most intimate relationship of our  lives.  She helped with the sequela of my ongoing treatments for leukemia and after she developed a rare type of pancreatic cancer during  COVID I helped her thru the cancer maze and found a radiation treatment that put her into remission. We were old and sick but having the time of our lives.  Some how it all became precious. Caring for each other deepened our intimacy and became a lovely part of our partnership. A privilege rather than a burden. She relapsed last year and we tried the radiation (PRRT) again and thought we had some more time. But only 6 months later she got very ill and we found she had a liver full of cancer. I took her home. We stayed side by side thru four long months and walked hand in hand everywhere. What a bittersweet time. I still feel her hand in mine.

articles.title: Dating Moves Fast in Your 70s
articles.summary: For our third date, he told me to bring my toothbrush.

comments.name: Jayda Banuelos
comments.body: Honestly, when Im watching TV shows it can be hard to catch my attention if the beginning is boring. My favorite TV shows are definitely Friends or The Vampire Diaries. I think out of the two, Vampire Diaries is my favorite. At first I tried to watch it but got really bored with the first few episodes. It's a show that has like 10 seasons and 23, hour long episodes for each season!  I decided again to watch it but this time truly sit down and watch it without getting bored. The first few episodes were again kinda boring, but the more I got into it the more I realized that this show was amazing! This show is about two vampire brothers who fall in love with the same girl, yet only the girl is a doppelganger to the girl they both fell in love with years ago! The Vampire Diaries includes people like Nina Dobrev, Ian Somerhalder, and Paul Wesly. Aside from the show being super amazing and interesting, the real life drama with these characters is so interesting too! I highly recommend this show to anyone who likes drama, romance, plot twists, and comedy. Coming from someone who gets bored easily and has a short attention spam, this show contains many different twist and turns, and is by far, my favorite show!

comments.name: Maria Villegas
comments.body: Out of all the Tv shows out there, Good Omens is definitely my most favorite show of them all. Good Omens began as a book co-written by Terry Pratchett and one other author (who turned out to be a bad person so I will not name them). The book grew a large fan base, especially in the UK where both the authors are from. The book was so loved in fact, that it got it's own BBC radio special, and a musical adaptation. Yet, beginning in May of 2019, the first season of Good Omens, was released. It stared Micheal Sheen as Aziraphale, and David Tennant as Crowley. The series very closely followed the book, where Aziraphale, the angle of the eastern gate of Eden, and Crowley, the demon who tempted Eve to eat the apple, live on earth reporting back to their respective sides. Then, Armageddon is announced and Aziraphale and Crowley decide to work together to save earth. Season 2 however, follows a different story. It is still about Aziraphale and Crowley, but now they are trying to solve a mystery that could change the world, while also following the development of their relationship. And because I really recommend watching the show, I will not spoil the ending of season 2, or what season 3 is about. The characters and plot are what bring me to loving this show. It changed how I saw so much of the world, and what relationships should be. The show is very queer accepting and represents people of many different backgrounds. Ultimately,  the show is amazing and meaningful to me.

comments.name: Amelia O'Connor
comments.body: Some of my favorite television shows of all time would have to be either South Park or Bojack Horseman. Very basic shows however they made such an impression on me and my view on life. I personally favored South Park, mostly the older seasons, as it made fun of all people and all things. Also, it’s hilarious. Then with Bojack Horseman I loved the characters in it and how the whole story was played out. I personally am way too indecisive and watch too much television to have a personal #1.

comments.name: Dion Cenga
comments.body: Many people have a lot of different TV shows, but there is just one that I admire. This TV show is called the Mentalist. I love this show because it has a lot of mysterious things to notice as well as justice and revenge throughout the show with different characters. This show brings in curiosity as well as a great setting, and there is always one thing you can’t figure out. When I first started watching I didn't really think much of it but when I got into it I really started to love it. It has all of my favorite genres and is very interesting. I highly recommend this show to everyone who loves to watch, Comedy, Crime, and anything related to solving mysteries. The main character is called Patrick Jane, he is one tough guy that figures out everything. This is why I love this show!

comments.name: Samantha Stuart
comments.body: Out of all the shows I have tried to watch, there are only a few I love, and will rewatch on a weekly basis: Shameless U.S., YOU, Big Mouth, and Friends. There are probably more, but these came to me the fastest. ‘YOU’ has definitely been my most recent obsession. Both the dramatic effect and the humorous narration make this show very bingeable. I have gotten through the first season in around two days, despite the length of the episodes. If you’re looking for a dramatic thriller with a bit of humor and romance, this is a great pick. ‘Friends’ is somewhat self explanatory. With one character from every personality, whether it be sarcastic, neat-freak, free-spirited, and more, it allows the watchers to relate to at least one character if not more. ‘Shameless U.S.’ is a chaotic dramedy show about a family living on the south side of Chicago, and siblings raising themselves in spite of their deadbeat father and runaway mother. What’s more, is that the themes in this show bring different perspectives to the audience and keep you hooked throughout the lengthy show (11 seasons). And finally, Big Mouth. In this show, a group of animated middle schoolers begin to be challenged by growing up and going through puberty. It is hilarious, relatable, and a bit graphic at times, but overall, an amazing show to binge watch. All of these shows, though some are silly and unrealistic, touch home in my life because they allow me to feel comforted, and they give me a good laugh when I need it.

comments.name: Samantha
comments.body: My favorite TV shows include, Supergirl with Melissa Benoist and One Tree Hill with Bethany Joy Lenz and James Lafferty. These shows made an impression on me because they are different from each other but every time I rewatch them I realize why I watch them over and over again. One Tree Hill is an original story made by Mark Schwahn, and in every season there is more and more to look forward to. While in Supergirl, there’s more action but not the type of glory action, the type of action that’s kid friendly but still mature for an audience that is in a young adult age. The characters in both of these shows have made a somewhat imprint on me because almost every time I watched them they keep getting better and better every watch. Whenever I want to rank shows, “[my] rankings won’t please everyone” (Engle), but they are my opinion and some might agree and some might not. If I were to pick my number one out of both of these I would pick One Tree Hill almost every time. The characters, storyline, and I just love the drama it presents.

comments.name: Sage
comments.body: Attack on titan is the best show ever. It made me literally no longer fear death. After watching it I had to sit outside while I cried my eyes out and I realized that if a bomb were to drop on me, I would be ok with that. Not because nothing matters and we are all doomed anyway, but because everything mattered, and I felt fulfilled in what I knew about the world. It's wonderfully written and wonderfully executed.I truly believe that if more people in power watched this show, that wars would end. Not all wars, but a lot of the tension between countries would finally be understood. It truly opens up your eyes to a new way of thinking about everything. There is a reason it's dubbed a great political anime. It absorbs you in a way no other show I have watched has. You think it's just about fighting titans? Come talk to me again in another 2 seasons.

comments.name: Eva L. Rodriguez
comments.body: I don’t often watch too many new shows, I’ve been rewatching the same shows since I was young and if I had to give a top 3, I would say these: Castlevania, Stranger Things, and The Pitt. These are very different but I love all three of them. The writing never fails to entertain me. I have watched these shows many times and never gotten bored. They made an impression on me due to the originality. I mean, I’m sure the creators were inspired by other stories they have seen, but they still did such a good job on making it their own and creating unique characters with a deep background. Right now, my number one is The Pitt. This was one of the shows ranked in The New York Times’s list, along with Stranger Things. The Pitt is very accurate to how an emergency room is, whether it’s situations, or how staff gets treated. Stranger Things, I would say is very creative, but I think I only enjoy it up to the 4th season. The last season was good, but I think everyone (including myself) just expected more in the writing since it was the finale. Overall, these three shows are my favorite for different reasons: they’re creative, interesting, and never feel like the same story.

comments.name: DD in LA
comments.body:
As harsh as it is, it seems the Australians have an effective anti-illegal immigration policy, keeping would be migrants on islands off the mainland. 
It's an ugly, "concentration camp" kind of approach, but it keeps immigration orderly and in very reduced numbers.

comments.name: Lila
comments.body: Reading this article made my blood boil—particularly the account of Mr. Abdul, the Eritrean who claims he fled his country to avoid conscription, yet passed through Sudan, Russia, Belarus, Latvia, and Belgium, before arriving in France. Five countries where the risk he claims to be fleeing would no longer apply. And now, not satisfied at the thought of being sent back to Latvia (where, as the article notes, he should have applied for asylum) he is trying to illegally enter Britain—banking on the fact that they’ll have a harder time deporting him. If he manages to get into Britain, he’ll just be another of the thousands of young, unskilled men flooding the country and straining its resources (and likely not assimilating). This is such flagrant abuse of the asylum and legal immigration systems that it’s no wonder the Far Right is growing more and more popular in Europe.

comments.name: Meg
comments.body:
Yes, the numbers are going down, but insufficiently. Home Office statistics on “small boat “ arrivals as of August 2026 included the following:
2018: 299 
2025: 41,500
2026: projected less than 30,000
A heartening improvement would be closer to the 2018 numbers.

The BBC reports that Wednesday, in one single day, 781 people (mostly young men, as usual, and generally from countries that are hostile, if not genuinely dangerous, to women) arrived on ten “small” boats. What the British government is foisting upon its citizens is incomprehensible to me. They could stop this if they wanted.

comments.name: Maisy
comments.body: So this story, like so much of the media coverage, largely misses the point.  WHY are migrants so desperate to get to the UK (leaving behind a France with better health care and generous benefits)?  What are the pull factors?  Relatives/friends already in the UK? English language employment with less risk of employers being fined for hiring undocumented workers? Instant access for everyone to the NHS, no papers necessary?  The UK should and must look inward to identify what it can do to reduce these pull factors — which will be politically unpopular — instead of trying to blame Europe for a problem entirely of its own creation.

comments.name: Peter D
comments.body: Articles like this should be required reading when someone asks how right-wing populism can be on the rise in Europe.

articles.title: Inside France’s Push to Stop Migrant Boats to Britain
articles.byline: Ségolène Le Stradic and Mark Landler
articles.summary: Thousands of migrants cross the sea between France and England each year, though numbers have fallen amid increased policing.

comments.name: John Patt
comments.body:
While climate deniers contribute substantially to our climate change problem, those who acknowledge climate change, but deny that we can do anything about it, and so do nothing, are also culpable.
Likewise, those who maintain that it is the government's responsibility to address climate change, and so make no personal effort, are exacerbating the problem.

comments.name: Jeff Sawyer
comments.body: A large part of the answer, if it's not too late, is to elect politicians who believe scientific evidence and offer scientific solutions but lose to profiteers who will find it convenient to ignore the facts until the day finally comes when country club grass cannot be greened up no matter how much water you give it.

comments.name: Mike Upstate NY
comments.body:
We don't travel in the summer anymore. The last time we traveled in the summer was 4 years ago. We thought that it would be clever to visit Ottawa, but it was in the 90s (f) all week.
We do take long weekends in our PHEV, and one trip overseas each year in March. It's chilly in places like Paris and London in March, but it's less crowded and less expensive (hotels, flights). Now, all that said, please don't follow my example. Continue to travel in the summer. Thank you.

comments.name: Nathan
comments.body: well informed article, thanks! the reality is that most Americans have long kissed any vacation goodbye, let's call it 'economic climate' of depressed wages and the constant grind to get money to make ends meet....being from the midwest, and in my 40's I do think that I might just see the day that migration reverses back to great lakes region for 'climate comfort'. a cloudy, rainy day, high of 45, and a cold winter is starting to look not so bad....

comments.name: Charles
comments.body: Now approaching age 80, I’m pleased that European jaunts (four of them) are part of my past. We did not know then that the 1960s & 70s would be part of a Golden Era of travel! But that is what happened — at least for this American.

comments.name: Tom Walker
comments.body: Stay-Vacations are the answer. Why fly thousands of miles to get a glass of wine in France or some pasta in Italy. Find your secret spot close to home and away from the crowds. You'll be more relaxed and happy. And isn't that what vacations are really for?

comments.name: Hamlet
comments.body:
I drive an EV, and spent almost $45k to put 38 solar panels on my roof. My carbon footprint is tiny, if I even have one. I feel like I've compensated for a flight once a year or every other year.

And I look at my neighbors, who drive two huge pickups with big V8 engines, who must spend a small fortune to fill their tanks. They cancelled their trip to Hawaii this fall because airfare was too high. Which means they will take one of those trucks on the road for their getaway. 

I just don't know...

comments.name: Ken
comments.body: I count myself as very lucky. I drove from Wisconsin to North Carolina in July. I missed the week of severe wildfire smoke from Canada, I missed the severe storms from the Carolina’s all along my route home through Indiana.

articles.title: Travelers Are Reckoning With the Ultimate Disrupter: Climate Change
articles.summary: Once dismissed as occasional inconveniences, climate-related disruptions are now an inescapable fixture of summer travel. How will travelers respond?

comments.name: Appaulled
comments.body: American Alcohol is still available in Alberta ( where I live) but most of us are simply not buying it. I check labels on everything I buy and if it is American, I forego it.i buy oranges from Australia, Egypt, South Africa, Peru, and Morocco and find the flavour quite good. The only thing I have trouble finding is Celery in the winter but can live without that. Most people I know are doing the same. My point is this boycott of American products is consumer driven and even items which are available are not being bought because of anger. This will likely not change even when American products are put on the shelves. Trump has turned many of us against American products because we feel that he is acting out his hatred of Canadians by hitting us economically and Americans seem fine with it.

comments.name: Edgar
comments.body: As a bourbon lover who lives in a state with a relatively limited selection, I am happy to see hard to find whiskey appearing on the shelves. The real question is why aren’t whiskey producers  already aware of this demand in other states? Bourbon manufacturers should be pivoting to this existing market.

comments.name: Kris
comments.body: Long time buyer of vintage goods. I have bought from Canada off and on for 25 years. I went to buy a vintage collection on ebay the other day. 100 %tarriff charge. Cost of item 167.90. import tax 167.90 ,. Thought it had to be an error so went back next day. Same tax.

comments.name: Bo
comments.body: Meh, I'll stick to bourbon, vs. blended

comments.name: Angus,Brother of Fergus
comments.body: Reading this at a pub on Salt Spring Island. I asked and was told no American liquor was on site. Was told at first there was a bit of concern from a few in the beginning of the tariff war. And then people just stopped asking for it. People just no longer want it and have gotten used to buying Canadian, Scottish, Irish, but nothing American for sale here. Not even the snacks are American, I just noticed that one and this place is packed.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body: So many words to say Bourbon is produced in red states showing Canada is targeting Trump voters. Banning Canadian Whiskey is just tit-for-tatting by the US.

comments.name: DB
comments.body: Could the author share any data supporting the claim that an expected boom in domestic sales for Canadian spirits never materialized? As written, it rests on a single quote, and the LCBO and SAQ have reported notable gains in Canadian whisky and spirits sales since the bans began.

articles.title: Why Do the Trade Wars Keep Coming for Your Whiskey?
articles.summary: As the U.S. prepares to ban imports of Canadian spirits, it’s worth examining the reasons a relatively minor commodity looms so large.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body: How to ruin a great economy handed to you by President Joe Biden.  And my god, Joes cadaver would be doing a better job for the American people.  Beyond any shadow of doubt.

comments.name: Rande Williams
comments.body: Rates are up, erratic tariffs tamp demand of units sold, and erratic policies stifle effective planning and disincentivize investment. Labor shortages threaten to supply shock foods and homes for sale. Home sales are a leading indicator - down. Stock funds rise on the coat tales of a few mega megs corporations owned by our oligarchy. The idiogarchy who made this idiocracy possible. A tech Guilded Age?  Hmmm. Are the idiogarchs pumping this market?  Who else would buy into an imminent recession?  More importantly, who blinks, and dumps first?  My $ is on Ellisons.

comments.name: Archibald
comments.body: Bond markets up, mortgage rates up, food prices up, 750,000 U.S. citizens stripped of health subsidies, gas prices and diesel at record highs, former friends and allies alienated, endless war with Iran, shameless graft and corruption at unprecedented levels . . . are voters “tired of so much ‘winning”yet”?

comments.name: FRK
comments.body:
Trump on gas prices:
“You have a little higher, you have a higher. It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done. Remember that it’s a little more. It’s even if it was, frankly, even if it was a lot more, but that’s gonna come tumbling down. That’s gonna be like a rocket ship in reverse,”

The man is totally divorced from reality. "It's a very inexpensive price for what we've done. All he's done with his unnecessary war is caused the deaths and injuries of many of our military personnel, wasted billions of dollars, depleted our supplies of precision weapons, raised diesel prices to record levels, raised gas prices, raised inflation, strengthened our enemies and weakened our allies.  

And Trump is bragging about accomplishing all of the above?  Even if you don't like democrats vote for them. Someone has to at least try to stop this madness the republicans are completely complicit in.

comments.name: Archibald
comments.body: How many times will the “invisible hand of the marketplace” have to suckerpunch Trump before it beats some sense into him?

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
This has nothing to do with inflation, it has a lot to do with instability. Trump and others have created an environment where commerce cannot function. Business need a quiet, stable environment to function. Inflation is the main story, but having this crises is caused by leaders in many countries and commerce cannot allow business to function normally. Trump contributes to this and he is one person who has to tune it down. A recession will wipe out pensions and cause the government to pay higher interest on borrowing when deficits are at historical levels. It is only a matter of time when the economy is weakened and the people lose value.

This is a problem caused by the leaders of the most powerful countries and the outcome will result in how they behave now!

comments.name: Andy
comments.body: How much of this strong job market is AI and data center build out?  Is there going to be a massive hangover when that burst of work finishes and jobs; manufacturing, construction, and servicing support for these computer warehouses, ends and the jobs AI replaces start being lost?  Seems like we're going to suffer through a decade or more of, as the Boss says, "feeling like we're on a downbound train".  It may well be that no matter what party rules after 2028, they're going to be pinned with that.

comments.name: Mark H
comments.body: the situation we're in now started in 2000 when George W. Bush became President. Instead of using the budget surplus to pay down the national debt, refund checks were sent and taxes started getting cut. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq got put onto the nation's credit card and taxes continued to get cut. 2008 should have been a wake-up call. Instead interest rates got cut and stayed too low for too long. Taxes continued to be cut while spending increased and the national debt kept growing. Now events are putting pressure on the economy and the bill is coming due in the form of higher interest rates and higher inflation. And the federal government isn't going to be able to avoid raising taxes. It can't cut spending any further to get out of this mess.

articles.title: Bond Markets Are Volatile and Oil Prices Rise
articles.summary: The rise came a day after a sharp sell-off in government debt.

comments.name: SamanthaWasMySpiritAnimal
comments.body: I totally agree- before I saw Diesel as a 'better Guess?' - now I am looking forward to seeing what Martens's full attention does for Margiela/MM6. For punk/denim, please cover the R13 shows :)

comments.name: Winthropo muchacho
comments.body:
Ella:

You go girl!

comments.name: Herb
comments.body: Marxists used to talk about "bourgeois decadence."  This show -- as well as this article -- offer vindication.

comments.name: Ho Hum
comments.body:
"He is leaving to focus on his other job as creative director of Maison Margiela"

Unfortunately, no, his work here is not "done."

Can't wait for the Maison Margiela moans and groans ... oy.

comments.name: JimmyMac
comments.body: If there is still the capacity for mirth in the future I can envision historians setting up watch parties to polish their snark. Still, nothing can beat the dubious street wear of the "70's.

comments.name: John Virgone
comments.body: Mirrors should be mandatory in the dressing rooms.

comments.name: jim
comments.body: Fashion??  Really??  I thought they were costumes for some upcoming TV show or movie or even an off-Bway show about a bunch of people who have hit rock bottom.

comments.name: Michael Lusk
comments.body: Some of the clothes I like, some I don't, but in some cases my reaction to the clothes is overwhelmed by my revulsion at the emaciated appearance of the models. The girls must be starving themselves to get that thin.

articles.title: Hot Pants, Hedonism and Heavy Breathing on the Runway
articles.summary: Glenn Martens goes out with a metaphoric bang at Diesel. But he leaves behind something even more attention-worthy.

comments.name: Mimi
comments.body: This is going to cost more than our tax dollars…if Hollywood doesn’t read the fine print they are going to be controlled (censored) by this tax break that we have to pay for. Given it’s going through, without any thought of us the taxpayers, at minimum this subsidy needs to CAPPED.

comments.name: Betsy
comments.body: David Ellison may not have it, too early to tell, but if he wants to really be a Hollywood leader (beyond heading two studios) he might try inspiring the film and TV industries with some far-sighted ideas and commitments rather than spouting the usual platitudes fellows like he are known for.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: One important factor that was not mentioned in the article is that the reason labor costs are so much cheaper for filming overseas is because their wages don't have to include allocation for union health benefits which can be substantial. Most of the countries where these movies are filmed provide free health care for their citizens (unlike the US) so  the playing field is mot level, even before the incentives are factored in.

comments.name: FISSIONFUSION
comments.body:
"The bill provides a tax credit of at least 20 percent on the wages of the vast array of workers who create movies and TV shows. That includes actors and directors as well as camera operators and makeup artists."

Starting a production company, tomorrow. Hiring film influencers, phone videologists, Ring Doorbellologists, overactors, actor-uppers, news/sports consumerologists, life consultologists (people alive), costume-ologists (people with clothes), makeupers (people with eye liner, lipstick, Plexaderm), propsologists (people with stuff), craft service-ologists (people with food). Apply within.

comments.name: Greg
comments.body:
....and who owns (will own if a merger is completed) most of the production? 
Ellison and Bezos. 
That is all we need to know to properly evaluate this potential legislation and who will be the biggest beneficiaries.

comments.name: Andrea
comments.body: The timing of this is incredibly suspect, on the heels of DA Bonta settling the Paramount Skydance/WB antitrust case, featuring Trump pals the Ellisons. That settlement included a court-enforceable clause that required increased domestically-created content output. Just days after that settlement, legislation is introduced and backed by the president to federally subsidize domestically-created content?

comments.name: Be great
comments.body:
Please listen carefully. I am a working member of the television community and I live in California. I work hard for a living and I am a “below the line “ employee. My fellow union members and I have so lost so much work to states like Georgia where the tax incentives are 30 percent. 
There are people who are losing their health insurance because they can’t make the days to meet the minimum. The companies that own these shows don’t care about people, they only care about the bottom line. It is awful. It trickles down to other industries like catering, prop and costume shops. Trucking, and other rentals. All we are asking for is to give similar deals to keep the work here in this state that empower so many people. This is not a handout. This is common sense. This industry has been here for 100 years. We want just keep our jobs and our homes.

comments.name: Peachy
comments.body: It's hard to reconcile the idea that the government of the United States of America is considering this type of subsidy when there are so many other higher priorities they should be focusing on that are already underfunded. Let's start with fully funding the arts and humanities, PBS, day care, FEMA responsiveness, reduce the federal debt, etc. then we'll talk.

articles.title: A Weary Hollywood Celebrates the Prospect of Federal Funding
articles.summary: In response to an exodus of movie and TV production, a bill is being introduced in Congress that would use tax credits to subsidize filming in the United States.

comments.name: Keith
comments.body: Chinese and other foreign business leaders look at America as an unsafe investment, a new era in international trade. We've allowed the President to act like a monarch who can nullify agreements that took years or decades to establish. The Canadian PM and Brazilian President clearly laid out the stakes that they are developing new supplies chains that does not include the U.S.

comments.name: Stephanie
comments.body: It appears as though the US government has forgotten that the whole point of a state visit isn’t to fluff Trump’s ego while focusing on superficial nonsense. Apparently, the people who used to focus on things like trade relationships and cooperation for the safety of the world against rogue technology have been reassigned to more pressing issues like arches and ballrooms.

comments.name: KfromCanada
comments.body: Maybe Vance saying, "We borrow money from Chinese peasants to buy the things those Chinese peasants manufacture.", was taken as an insult by China? I would think that comments such as that certainly don't help to make good diplomatic relationships between countries.

comments.name: BlueIguana
comments.body: Trump's State Dinner for PRC Chairman Xi Jinping was a beautiful event.  We watched Xi raise his glass several times and say "gan bei!" to the White House dinner guests.  Despite Trump's illegal ban on the U.S. press, the event was well covered and Xi and Madame Peng Liyuan were made welcome at The White House.  Xi's brief visit to the U.S. ends today.  Xi has undoubtedly noticed a change in President Trump since Trump visited him a year ago in Beijing, and since he visited the U.S. at Mar-a-Lago in 2017.   Obviously Trump's plans for a huge new ballroom and his  Arch of Triumph 'military complex' are pipe dreams.

comments.name: C Charles
comments.body:
Having worked and traveled extensively in China oh, about 25 years or so ago, I can tell you the Chinese are always teaching you a lesson. 

They are extremely gracious in this way. I have to say I have terrific fondness of the country and its people. If you are invited to tea, that’s a lesson. If you are taught a few words, in exchange for a few words of English, that’s a lesson. If none of these things happen, another lesson you really ought to pay attention to. Subtle, these lessons, but always, something to learn.

Now, whether you choose to listen to the lesson coming from some of this planets most gracious and civilized people is entirely up to you. 

Does anyone in the uh administration within the range of my words get the lesson? I don’t think they even attempted the homework, they all had tutors for that.

comments.name: S Venkatesh
comments.body: Atleast US Media could finally observe & report on One Glaring In-your-Face difference between Trump & President Xi understanding of their respective people’s strength. When Trump visited China in May, with a line-up of top US Business leaders in tow (Nvidia’s Chief had to catch Air Force One in Alaska !), President Xi did not receive him at the Airport. At the end of Trump’s visit there was No Joint Communique, leave alone the customary Joint Press Conference. When President Putin visited China the very next week, President Xi made it a point to welcome him in Identical pomp as Trump. Putin’s visit ended with a grand public unveiling of a Detailed Joint Communique & Joint Press Conference. President Xi was accompanied by only a few Politburo Members & the Foreign Minister for his US visit. President Xi clearly showed the Whole World that it is the United States which needs to kowtow to China for Trade (Tariffs, Minerals, AI) & Security (Iran, Ukraine, North Korea) favours. Sadly, neither US Media nor the American people feel the Shame of having to play second fiddle to China on the World stage.

comments.name: Nunpa Cetan
comments.body: Xi Jinping didn't bring Chinese CEOs because he already knows that Chinese companies have outstripped American companies in the fields that matter: EVs, AI, et al. Chinese products are no longer second best and haven't been so in a long time. While Trump takes us back to the past, China is taking us 'back to the future'. Why waste time coddling the U.S. when everything else is falling into place for China worldwide? The absence of Chinese CEOs is telling. And a two-month extension of the economic truce between the two countries is immaterial, merely confirmation that the only way the Trump admnistration can create growth is by taxing imports.

comments.name: Sirfreakin
comments.body:
This is no surprise . The whole world has an unofficial moratorium on dealing with America. Making a deal with this administration means nothing or something, tomorrow maybe. “I don’t like the way they look so I’m changing my mind.”
When the attributes of honesty and trustworthiness return to American maybe others will engage. In the meantime we watch the ship sink into mediocrity.
China seems more occupied by racing past the US which postures with insincerity.

articles.title: Missing From the Trump-Xi State Dinner: China’s Business Leaders
articles.summary: American chief executives turned out in force to see Xi Jinping, while their Chinese counterparts were absent, a sign of how drastically business ties have changed.

comments.name: Khalid
comments.body:
A nothing burger. What is preventing the police from releasing the report about if he assisted the banker.  A prominent banker asks a contact who happens to be Justice member on law advice and gets directed to a law firm. 

Come on Brazil it’s a IQ test. Don’t fall for Bolsonaro 2.0

comments.name: Sue
comments.body: Election meddling by the U.S.?  Probably a pretty decent chance that the DJT administration would stoop to that. No reason to disregard it out of hand.

comments.name: Rick All
comments.body: I applaud the journalist that wrote this article. She was able to depict the scandal relationships of Supreme Court Ministers with the current Brazilian government. The involvement of Mr Moraes and his wife with Mr Vorcaro is something that would immediately impeach him. I wished the journalist could also provided a bit more information of how the Brazilian congress is also ineffective ( to say the least) and complicit with all the “ horror show” that is Brazilian politics today. The worst of all is that ,In the coming election, people will have to choose between a populist leftist that put Brazil 25 years  behind all other emerging countries and spend the public funds in populist aids or a right wing guy who  loves Trump and admire Bukele. Sad….

comments.name: Jupiter
comments.body: The Vorcaro scandal has proved to be the largest web of corruption Brazil has ever seen. The findings of numerous investigations have been kept secret, and the info that’s been released so far has been released in a very selective manner. To the Brazilian voters, the most serious issue (and one that should be fully explained before elections are held) is: Flavio Bolsonaro, the candidate of the extreme right, is the only presidential candidate involved in Vorcaro’s dirty schemes. Flávio can be heard on a VM he left on Vorcaro’s phone begging for the remainder of a $130 million BRL (-$25 million USD) contribution to fund a biopic on the elder Bolsonaro… How deep is Flavio involved in Vorcaro’s scheme??? comments.name: David

This entire so called scandal has been invented by Bolsonaro and his son who are trying to seize power again. They are corrupt and will do anything to regain power. Bolsonaro is also supported by trump and is called the "trump of the tropics". 
I truly hope Brazilians do not fall for these lies. Lula has proven time and again he is a good and fair President who cares about his people. Bolsonaro is like trump! Something no one wants! A military dictator who tried to overthrow a fair election....BEWARE of Bolsonaro!

comments.name: LW
comments.body: Perhaps Brazil would be better off if everybody mentioned in the article were in prison, regardless of which corrupt faction they're part of.

comments.name: Greg
comments.body: Moraes is himself an enemy of democracy. Glenn Greenwald has done invaluable reporting on this from Brazil for years, and he has been a fair critic of both Lula and Bolsonaro.

articles.title: The High-Stakes Corruption Scandal Shaking Up Brazil’s Election
articles.summary: Allegations embroiling the Brazilian judge who jailed former President Bolsonaro are reshaping an election that has consequences for Latin America and Washington.

comments.name: Ren
comments.body: It’s been so disheartening to watch the Anti-Defamation League’s descent from an important antisemitism watchdog to a group that calls Macklemore antisemitic for calling for an end to, yes, the genocide in Gaza and the West Bank. As many have pointed out, when you call criticism of Israel and Zionism “antisemitism,” you conflate Judaism with supporting Israel’s genocide in Gaza, essentially forcing people who are against genocide to “be antisemitic.” Ditto to Robert Kraft calling what Macklemore said “hate speech”—you get to a point of irreconciliability: you’re saying that by speaking out about genocide someone is perpetuating hate speech, well, I guess I’m on the side of hate speech now…? To combat true antisemitism, these groups like the ADL really need to reconsider their definitions and semantics; calling pro-Palestine speech antisemitic will, unfortunately for them, not stop people from speaking out about Palestine and will make a lot more people willing to accept the label of “antisemitic.” It dilutes the meaning of antisemitic where people don’t feel like it’s a bad thing to be, if you say it’s antisemitic to call for an end to ruthlessly bombing children. See how that works?

comments.name: Francesca
comments.body: Bless him for giving his energy and time.  I still can't understand how people can disparage anyone callling for peace.  I also can't understand how Americans don't realise how much their entertainment culture is owned and censored...

comments.name: Robin
comments.body: People like Macklemore who blame everything on Israel (and U.S. support of it) while letting Hamas off the hook are actually hurting, not helping, innocent Gazans. The "Free Palestine" folks see this very long, complicated conflict through an overly simplistic, distorted prism of "oppressor vs oppressed." But it's not even remotely that simple. I have yet to see the "Free Palestine" crowd loudly and publicly denounce Hamas for its endless barbaric treatment of innocent Gazans. They seem oblivious to the fact that Hamas will gladly sacrifice every innocent man, woman, and child in Gaza in order to achieve its goal: destroy Israel and Judaism, and expand its repressive theocracy where all people are denied fundamental human rights. It's fine to point fingers at Israel's current horrible right-wing government; I sure do. But those who don't also equally denounce Hamas terrorists, who hid in tunnels they built beneath schools and hospitals, with money that should have gone to building Gaza's infrastructure, are not pro-Palestine at all, and are doing nothing to help innocent Gazans living under Hamas’s terrorist rule.

comments.name: kagni
comments.body: It seems that many supporters have no idea about the history of Palestinians in Gaza. The recent history is that Israeli government in 2005 removed Israeli farmers and opened Gaza to Palestinians who have been put in camps by Egypt since 1948.  The hope was that Gazans would thrive growing  fruit and vegetables. Instead Hamas was elected and spent huge donations of money ( $40M/ month from Qatar) on the tunnel infrastructure while Gazans remained poor.  Hamas caused isolation of Gaza. Hamas declared goal is to kill Jews. You can look it up. So the people who feel sympathy for the Palestinians in Gaza ought to fight Hamas not Israel or Jews.

comments.name: Montana resident
comments.body: I guess I will now become a fan of rap. Macklemore, schedule some shows out here in Montana!

comments.name: Allison Schy
comments.body: If this isn’t the definition of riding on the success of someone’s hugely famous coattails, I don’t know what is.

comments.name: David--Philly
comments.body:
I never even heard of him or Ed Sheeran until getting thrown off the concert tour. 

Macklemore won a public relations coup d'tat. If he said nothing about Palestine, or if Kraft had not 
booted him off, the concert would be business as usual. 

He will be cleaning up in future concerts and music sales. 
 
David Philly

comments.name: Jean
comments.body: This situation reminds me of the fable of the fate of the bat, who couldn't decide whether he was a bird or a land animal, so he was banished to live alone and only come out at night. Sometimes you have to take a stance. Sheeran didn't and was left standing alone on the stage. Macklemore did and is now reaping the rewards.

articles.title: Macklemore Announces ‘Free Palestine’ Tour
articles.summary: The rapper, who was pulled from Ed Sheeran’s tour last week over his support for Palestinians, announced plans for three European dates.

comments.name: Mara
comments.body: i think our hearts have a special place for animals especially animals with a something special like Jimothy I personally haven't seen much of Jimothy online, but he is adorable. and i agree with many others that we have the instinct to help and this brings us together as a community because we all find something we love together.

comments.name: Foster Garonzik
comments.body:
PUNCH! My favorite celebrity animal. Every celebrity animal comes with a unique and intriguing back story. For example, my guy punch had gotten separated from his parents and used a stuffed animal to pretend it was his parents, aw so cute. But every celebrity animal isn’t all the same. Sure, you can see monkeys that look like Punch, but you won’t see your average trash can racoon like Jimothy. I mean what can I say, a neckless racoon? That’s quite astonishing. 
I mean the list goes on and on for these types of things. Every time something becomes an internet sensation it’s just a wonderful sight to see in today’s world because these animals come from everywhere. I doubt in the busy city of Philadelphia I will see a neckless racoon! But nonetheless, these animals are natural phenomononns and a brilliant sight in today's world!

comments.name: Leyla
comments.body: I absolutely love animals, never mind celebrity animals. But I honestly couldn’t pick just one. I even own semi celebrity animals! For 2 years, I have fostered kittens – and with a new litter of kittens every 2 months I decided it would be fun to post them on social media  and I now have like 10k followers. Not enough watch hours to generate any income but it's still fun. A year ago, my friend and I were obsessed with Punch the monkey and my little sister even had the Ikea stuffed animal. Even though I think the animals listed in the article are cute, my favorites are the animals of my own.

comments.name: Cleome Skema-Plume
comments.body: I have not been following any celebrity animals and barely knew they existed, but I did hear a little bit of a podcast about Jimothy and it sounds like people really like celebrity animals and it sounds like a really nice thing. I think having people fall in love with animals helps them want to take care of animals more and that's a thing we really need.

comments.name: oskar
comments.body: I think that animals that have become viral because of the natural instinct to connect and step in one's shoes, all of these online celebrities share one thing in common, all of these animals went through a change, or a struggle, or just are cute and grab hearts, they teach us to not look down on our hardships and embrace life to the fullest.

comments.name: Benjamin Jiang
comments.body: I personally think that the “celebrity animals” got so popular because they were cute, people love animals, and after it gets more and more popular, more people will know about it, possibly spread it to other people, and in return, it will become even more popular. Even as a person who loves animals, I’m surprised that a raccoon made it on the stage. I kind of feel bad for the animal since it has a disability and is being ridiculed online even though it knows nothing about it.

comments.name: Amelia O'Connor
comments.body: I think animals like Jimothy, Moo Deng, Punch, or Chonkers have become so popular on social media because they are all one of a kind and have never been seen in the world before. For instance, Jimothy is a raccoon but what makes him any special, why is he so popular on social media? Well he’s a hunchback and no one has ever seen a hunchback racoon therefore the people are amazed by it, interact with it, then the algorithm pushes it to more people. And with Moo Deng, she has an attitude, people love that diva type vibe from her, or with Punch for instance he carried a monkey with him all the time, and then with Chonkers he was just a thicker kind of seal. These special characteristics are entertaining for people around the world and that boosts the chance of people to see the videos of these viral animals. I think they say that we love things that we don’t usually see and we can have strong opinions on things. I’d say that they can teach us that being unique is always better than being just like anyone else.

comments.name: Eli Topaz

Also you can feel many emotions like sadness as they fight punch a lot and the attention he was getting on social media was massive and deserved.

Despite all the other drawbacks of NYC schools,  exposure to culture and other things NYC is known for should not be one of the things that students miss out on. comments.name: Lillie

comments.name: Orange & Blue

And certainly in light of the day-to-day multiple issues he faces that do get his attention & follow-through action. He shows diverse and unboxed-in thinking as a young Mayor that's refreshing. Reaching out with this ticket giveaway to those NY'ers who normally wouldn't have the opportunity to attend the opera. That has nothing to do with policy and everything to do with quality if life for the people. There's no such thing as too much visibility especially in a city as large & diverse as ours! He and his aids got it figured out on a regular basis.

comments.name: Vicky

It's great that they're giving free opera tickets away. But I wish Mamdani didn't have to be the face of everything.

I also see him doing recycling ads, on electronic bus kiosks, when I get in a cab. Endlessly when the World Cup was here. Shoveling snow for 30 seconds.

comments.name: Jonathan Drake
comments.body:
The beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24, 2026, in St. Louis, Missouri, has generated significant controversy and debate among observers regarding his historical legacy and the nature of the ceremony itself, and rightly so. 

Critics have raised serious objections concerning his administrative record, specifically pointing to concerns regarding his handling of abuse allegations during his tenure as Bishop of Rochester in the 1960s and questions surrounding institutional accountability. 

And, of course, he aided and abetted the Red Scare, and attacked LGBTQ citizens, claiming they were all going to Hell. 

Additionally, the large-scale event at the Dome at America's Center has drawn scrutiny over its commercialization, including high-tier sponsorship packages promoted by the Sheen Foundation. Critics contend that framing a solemn spiritual recognition as a high-profile, ticketed stadium event detracts from the traditional emphasis on pastoral humility.

comments.name: D
comments.body: I believe in the poetic truth of miracles, the divine, and holy lives that are recognized in beatification by the Church.

comments.name: Bill B.
comments.body: Fulton Sheen died in 1979, more than 30 years before that newborn was revived by doctors and nurses. I very much doubt that praying to a long-dead person had much to do with it.  For that 16-year-old to parade next to Sheen's jawbone feels pretty grotesque. Very weird.

comments.name: Pia

Research him.
Very elucidating.

comments.name: Brooklyn

comments.name: CliffsideCounselor
comments.body: The American Bar Association not only accredits law schools, it functions as a critical standard setter in terms of attorneys' competence, integrity, and conduct so as to uphold the Rule of Law, and to empower their private clients to stand up to an overbearing government.  It is not surprising that this blatantly corrupt US president, and his blatantly corrupt and sycophantic administration wants to basically kill the ABA as a regulator of our legal profession--which frankly is the envy of the world.  Shakespeare recognized the critical role of lawyers in upholding the rights of an individdual in law and society when he wrote:  "The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers" ( Henry VI, Part 2 (Act IV, Scene 2)).  The line is spoken by Dick the Butcher, a follower of the rebel leader Jack Cade.  Cade is leading a violent, anti-establishment revolt to overthrow the government and seize the crown.  Far from being an insult to lawyers, the quote is actually a backhanded compliment. The rebels realize that to establish total lawlessness and tyranny, they must first eliminate the legal professionals who defend the rule of law, order, and civil rights.   Keep in mind that this lawless, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administraiton also wants to strip STATES of their power to license attorneys.  Why??  So, that the Trump Administration can use crooked ones without impunity...or fear of disbarment.  The ABA is a critical pillar in our democracy--no question.

Its convoluted requirements for law school accreditation, its refusal to even consider conforming to the Bologna Process (thereby reducing a significant barrier to access for new lawyers - the unnecessary third year of law school and its concomitant financial burden), its insistence on adding to the already gratuitously onerous requirements for accrediting law schools, have made it a morally bankrupt gatekeeper for the legal profession. After four years as an Air Force officer my son decided to attend law school. His LSAT to low to get into the higher ranked schools. He had to attend a small private school. comments.name: vinbiko
comments.body: Everything about this idea makes sense. It is not surprising that the idea comes from a Swedish company/individual. Setting up such a grid allows maximum individualism while still supporting the community (the Nordic theory of love from the book, The Nordic Theory of Everything by Anu Partanen). However, I'm afraid this will have disastrous results in the US. The "haves" will have excellent service and a stable grid, while the "have nots" will be left to their own devices, and predatory mini companies will exploit them. Chalk this up to the toxic individualism that is "valued" in the US>

comments.name: Fredrik
comments.body: When in high school I visited the Tvind mølle in Denmark being developed, so Iwanted to make my own from oil drum cut in half. My parents erected a flag pole on the hill instead. Years later in the eighties we failed to get a Danish windmill built here locally. So in the mid nineties instead I asked Vattenfall (main utility company) to set up an electricity contract specifically for wind power. They agreed and our household was first in Sweden with this setup. In the advent of hourly metering in early 2000’s, I was finally able to get the electricity from our part owned windmills 500 km away, transferred to our house. And this is still how it works.

comments.name: One European
comments.body: The guy is on the right track, huge powerplants and several hundred KiloVolt grids are really vulnerable and a lot of people would be without power if either one is having problems. Decentralised production and small ring fed grids are much more resilient. A failure would affect less people and in a crisis situation the entire grid would not go out.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: Decentralized energy is definitely the way to go in all ways. A huge part of the struggle will be (political) to grasp the power from the hands of Big Energy corporations. The sun belongs to every individual, unlike oil, gas and other extractive material. There is no downside; there is only downside to NOT going in this direction. The closer you can get the power to the consumer, the more efficient, more secure and lest costly it will be to generate energy. Imagine how many trillions of $'s will be saved on energy extraction/production/usage. We need to elect officials who grasp the opportunity and are willing to wrestle the power away from big corporations.

comments.name: Jen
comments.body:
Guys - Have we not heard of Microgrids? These have been around for nearly 20 years and only need wider adoption to make reliable, cleaner energy a reality. They typically work on a loop at the neighborhood or community level, have a local battery park to store excess energy and use that excess after the sun goes down. Every house has solar and a system to convert / distribute the energy throughout the home.

I worked on one called BlockEnergy that Lennar put at the community level in South Florida. It has a 99% uptime average- even during storms.

This could be our reality. The utility companies could install this and maintain the equipment (just like they do the power lines now) - except we’d no longer need the power lines en-mass for every neighborhood anymore.

Business parks can also be put on Microgrids. 

It’s worth looking into folks. It works amazingly well.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
Good topic, but the article is thin on the technical and financial challenges of small power grids. Data packets and high voltage electricity are not the same thing. 

Large grids are large because economy of scale makes them cheaper to operate. For many decades, utilities have maintained sub-grids for hospitals and other critical infrastructure (able to disconnect and operate independently on diesel generators). 

What has changed is that power *generation* is shifting from large point-sources (coal fired plants, hydroelectric dams) to distributed sources (gas-fired plants, wind, and solar). That creates new opportunities, but those come with challenges.

comments.name: Donna
comments.body: Not sure why this is considered groundbreaking. Microsoft grids and local energy networks are already operating in other parts of the world including the UK.What we need is for residential consumers of power to have more optionality and choice.

comments.name: Ross
comments.body:
It's simply common sense that with the means we now have of producing electricity - helical wind-powered generators, bio-gas turbines, water, etc. - we should be producing electricity where it is needed; the giant power stations with concomitant grid only exist these days for the financial benefit of the giant power companies.
For small towns and villages as well as multi-occupancy buildings combined heat/power units are also a very sensible solution.

I live in a part of north-eastern Germany where the extremely beautiful landscape is being covered in gargantuan wind turbines and the electricity produced then transferred to the other end of the country via newly constructed HT pylons/cables, whereby a great deal of that electricity dissipates. This is totally ridiculous! Sustainable energy production and use requires producing power where it is needed!

articles.title: The World Needs Better Power Grids. Why Smaller May Be Better.
articles.summary: Jonas Birgersson, a Swedish entrepreneur, wants to use decentralized networks modeled on the internet to transform how electricity is distributed.

comments.name: Zezee

comments.name: Sarah Lyall
comments.body: It was a pleasure to learn about the life of Edward Lehner, who did so many thing but will forever be remembered for the sense of civic responsibility (and humor) he brought to the messy issue of dog poop. It's rare that one law can change the tenor of a city, and improve residents' quality of life, so thoroughly. (And it was an unexpected delight to learn of former Mayor Koch's zealous, umembarrassed efforts to enforce the law on what he called "dog doo.")

comments.name: D Bean
comments.body: It was gradual, but the change in behavior took place. I can't comment on just how bad it still is in NYC, but most other towns and cities followed the lead and things are immeasurably better. For the odd occasion that you step in the "doggy doo", I recommend scanning the nearby gutters for a lost bristle from a street sweeper. These steel strips are the best tool for cleaning your shoe.

comments.name: Diane F.
comments.body:
I'm a dog owner, and see many piles of dog poop left by irresponsible dog owners, but I have never heard  "it would be physically challenging to hold onto a dog while simultaneously collecting its waste."
The real reason is laziness, irresponsibility, and entitlement. I never miss an opportunity to loudly call out any dog walker who walks away without picking it up. Whip out your phone, then post their photo on Facebook, or wherever. Public shaming does work.

comments.name: ThinkingAboutThis
comments.body: Scraping your shoe on a curb, using a twig to pick poop out from between boot treads, closing the last car door only to realize that somebody in the car had stepped in it, dog poop was simply part of our collective youth experience (M, 69). Oh yes- and barefoot summers invariably meant a wrong step squeezing up between your toes. Green bags are better.

articles.title: Edward Lehner, Who Made Dog Owners Pick ‘It’ Up, Dies at 93
articles.summary: Before the law passed, navigating New York was a harrowing exercise in dog-feces avoidance. As he put it, sometimes “you would come home and have it all over you.”

comments.name: Ari
comments.body: I friend shared a video (prior to AI) where a male/buck deer plays with a soccer ball alone in a field and purposely knocks it into the net.  After he scores, he jumps for joy enthusiastically just like a human player.  No doubt he had previously watched kids playing from the adjacent woods.  It is honestly one of the most touching moments I’ve ever seen.

comments.name: JRO
comments.body:
I am seldom surprised but always impressed by the fascinating and ingenious animal kingdom.
The presumption that only humans can have language,  complex societal structures and show compassion and intelligence is utterly wrong.  
Raccoons are awesome!

comments.name: Purple Spain
comments.body: Raccoons are intelligent adaptive creatures with extraordinary dexterity.  They use their front paws to wash their food, feed themselves, and then wash their hands like little humans.  (This is why the water bowl gets so filthy overnight.)   As for sipping margaritas, if it’s good enough for the humans, it’s good enough for us.

comments.name: Jane
comments.body: I live on a couple of acres in a wooded area, and a momma raccoon and her grown kits come to my back door in the evenings (wanting food). I have a momma kitty and her grown kittens inside. The momma raccoon stares inside with apparent fascination watching me play with the kitties. If I open the door to give the raccoons some food, the momma raccoon acts like she wants to come inside to join the kitties. The momma raccoon and kits also play on my back deck like happy puppies. Reading this article makes me want to see if they would play with a cat toy.

comments.name: Flaneuse duBois
comments.body: Great piece, I laughed out loud multiple times!  Not least about the drunk mama raccoon.  Fascinating!!  I wanted to do field biology when I was in college, I might have stuck with it if I could sit at a Mexican resort and watch adorable little raccoons do ingenious things.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
@ poslug cambridge Yes. And you don't have to go to Mexico to see that. In back of the bldng Iived in Clifton, NJ there was a tribe of cats living in a little strip of woods behind the parking lot on one side and the highway on the other. Often you would see deer with their noses against the fence ogling the cars in the lot and you wondered what the attraction was. One nt the usual suspects were eating out of the cans of cat food a concerned neighbor had placed out there as usual (I couldn't be as extravagant and left dry food). What happens is that some residents move on and just abandon cats there and I noticed a slightly bigger coat on one. When I approached he/she turned and hissed at me: a really large raccoon. Have to admit it was a thrill to see something wild 'sill living in the county'. 
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: Barbara
comments.body:
Fortunately it appears that the sale of little turtles - at the 5-and-10, etc - that was so popular back in the 50s (and 60s?) has ended. I hope so. 
At the same time, as a kid in a very rural area, i hed a turtle " pet" - a wild turtle who lived entirely freely outdoors, though ii made him a little nest with a cardboard "house " for when it rained (applying human standards...). He actually did use it, i suppose to hide and rest...
In turn, he kept our breezeway free of flies and other annoying bugs , that to him were,  i suppose. succulent morsels. 
My mean neighbor (daughter in a very troubled family) tried to kill him twice. The second time, she succeeded, as I found him dead in the field.
It was experiences like this that always have made me skeptical of the supposed "superiority" of humans. We're all just creatures - though yes, we humans can choose to use our gift of life for good or ill.

For the love of God, please! Enough with the social media influencer videos! Nobody cares!

NYC is many, many things, the most prominent of which is her authentic self. She is like no other city and her streets are not cookie-cutter copies plaguing so many other urban areas. Very interesting article, but a bit light on details of history.
Pre-revolutionary France was not just a Catholic society, it was a  kindom where the High Clergy was ABOVE the king in status: the First Estate. Two successive cardinals, Richelieu and Mazzarin, helped consolidate the French kingdom and check the power of Catholic Spain and the Hapsburgs. Both were richer than the king himself. 
From the end of the 18th century until mid-20th, the French Church was associated with at least 3 attempts to overthrow the Republic. It's control over state bureaucracy, high Officer Command, and education was formally ended after the Dreyfus Affair. Until 10 years ago, the far-rightist Front national party held Traditional Latin Mass at the ends of its annual party convention -- just to defy Vatican II popes in power.

Having problems with this wording: "the technique has also become a way for companies to collect data from technologies built by others."

I don't think the technique collects *data*: it collects *knowledge". Hinton's paper is specifically titled "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network."

"Knowledge" refers to the fact that the network "knows" what to do with data; it has developed network paths that optimize data according to users' criteria. AI systems are not "data"; they are programs that process data.

Flippantly and uncreatively declaring that people should just stay home doesn't solve anything nor is it remotely realistic. comments.name: Stephan
comments.body:
I see we are pretending the UN is a world Government that can order and demand. It isn't and it's not going to be. 

As for those calling for the expulsion of the US, Russia, Israel, etc... etc... What exactly will that accomplish? Will the UN be able to impose its will on them? Will the UN send in the World Police? Or perhaps send in the UN Army? 

The UN doesn't have the authority or the ability it isn't a World Government really. Neither is International Law meaningful unless nations are WILLING to obey it. It's unenforceable...
How long ago did China tell the UN to blow it out its ... over the South China Sea? And how much has China cared about UN pronouncements?
Laws that can't enforced aren't Laws they're jokes.

The UN has no way to enforce anything unless the Nations are willing to send their armies to die for the UN. And what Nation is going to send their army to die for Hamas or invite Nuclear destruction by invading the US to enforce UN decrees? 

In terms of real world power? The Flat Earth society probably has more than the the UN.

comments.name: Hamid Varzi
comments.body:
"So, what I’m hearing you say is that the U.N. is still a useful talking shop. But perhaps no longer itself involved in conflict resolution?"

Almost a rhetorical question. Until the UNSC is radically altered, or eliminated altogether, no major conflict can ever be resolved. No single nation should have the ability to veto resolutions that are often supported by up to 90 % of the world's population. Moreover, if a UNSC Resolution is unanimously passed the U.N. should send its peacekeepers in to execute the Resolution,  as in the case of Israeli settlements. We cannot go on seeing one country protecting another against the wishes of 95 % of the General Assembly.

comments.name: Realist
comments.body:
The U.N. has proved itself to be a feckless, toothless organization many times over many decades regarding too many incidents to list here.

Currently, however, it should have threatened Russia with expulsion when Putin invaded Ukraine.  At the very least it should have removed Russia from the Security Council.  The same expulsion threat should have been levied against Israel and the U.S. for their criminal  war against Iran and Trump's endless threats to multiple sovereign nations. 

I've said for far too many years that for the U.N. to have any meaning it needs a million soldier standing army ready to deploy against ANY aggressor nation.  Never happen, of course and the U.N. will remain a meaningless waste of space on the East River of Manhattan.

comments.name: arvay
comments.body:
After the current US president, from its podium, clarified the fact that not only has the US repeatedly violated the UN Charter — but rejects the organization's core principles — the US must be expelled from the United Nations. 

Let's be clear: it is no exaggeration to state that Trump has capped a post-WW2 series of interventions and military actions with alignment with ihe "values"of the criminals  convicted at Nuremberg — a judgement  that set stage for creation of the UN.

Crimes against peace, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and conspiracy to commit these crimes— these were what their crimes were — and Trump just blatantly endorsed them —  hurled them in the faces of the assembled nations of the world.

How can countries who accept the UN Charter and presumably attempt to live by its precepts sit in the same room with THAT?

comments.name: Hank G
comments.body:
I've seen every English speaking episode of Survivor from all countries. I've never missed an episode since I was 10 in 2010. I love Survivor and I feel that Jeff Probst consistently dismisses us, Survivor's most passionate fans. There's good reason why we criticize Jeff and his twists. 

This interview shows that Jeff doesn't understand the fundamental appeal of The Television Show Survivor. The appeal is The Game of Survivor itself.

The Game of Survivor is to vote each other off an island until 2 (or 3) remain and then get the eliminated contestants to pick a winner from the Survivors. That's it. It was created by Charlie Parsons in 1990s.

We only watch The Television Show "Survivor" for the The Game of Survivor itself. The decisions required by the Game of Survivor naturally creates wonderful a television show. Complex stories consistently emerge out of The Game like magic. The simplicity is beautiful and endless entertaining. Occasionally, the stories are slow and boring (Survivor 5), but that's reality. That's the brilliance of reality TV. 

When Jeff says "The Game is a device for The Television Show," it is incredibly disheartening. He doesn't trust his audience. He doesn't trust The Game by itself.

Every twist, every diversion, every distraction designed by Jeff is a panicked ego-trip. Jeff has been a terrible steward for The Game of Survivor and it has deeply hurt the quality of The Television Show Survivor.

Joe and Jon... wow! You're both FANTASTIC interviewers. 

Our family has been watching Survivor together for so many years that it has become part of our family story. So many seasons, so many conversations, laughs, debates, predictions—and so many memories made together around this show. When we started watching, our oldest son was 3 or 4; he's 30 now.

Jeff, I don’t think I’ve ever stopped to say thank you for that. For all the years of storytelling, adventure, and moments that brought our family to the same couch, season after season. What a gift that has been.

comments.name: Mac
comments.body:
Travel safe, TSA accepted trauma shears would be nice. 

Quite a lot of people are on either blood thinners (e.g., Eliquis (apixaban), Xarelto (rivaroxaban), Warfarin (Coumadin)) or anti-clotting drugs (e.g. Plavix (clopidogrel), Pradaxa (dabigatran)) or unwisely low-dose aspirin.  These can lead to serious nosebleeds and hard to stop bleeding from what would otherwise be minor cuts. So it is highly advisable if you know someone on these drugs to keep band-aid type plasters with a clotting agent (Curad makes one), nosebleed stoppers (e.g., Nampons®) and Hemostatic Gauze. I’ve seen a really bloody incident at the gym driven by these medications.

comments.name: AnotherCitizen
comments.body:
"But who do you lock up if the intrusion was the work of an A.I. model acting without the permission of its human operators?"

The answer is obvious: the CEO. If a chief executive is held personally responsible for negative behavior, just as they are held responsible for positive financial performance with increased compensation and bonuses, they will be highly motivated to create and manage their organization in a way that reduces the risk of illegal behavior. Yes, treat CEOs as if they themselves committed the illegal behavior, including jail time if that would be the punishment for an individual committing the offense. As the buck stops with them when it comes to positive performance,  so too should it stop with them when it comes to illegal behavior. 

Fines and other means of punishment of the organization itself will not provide as strong of an incentive for leaders to ensure legal behavior as personal, both criminal and civil, legal liability and risk will.

This should be the standard for all illegal corporate behavior, not just limited to AI.

Is it not possible simply to define the assigned "task" as NOT including hacking?

comments.name: Lois
comments.body:
I have a question for the journalists or anyone else who can answer it.  Why would AI Agents create a religion as two separate groups have done?  Is it just some hackers joke on the rest of us?  
On a whim,  I created a thought experiment and asked the Google unnamed AI search agent, This question:  "If I created a science fiction story about Jesus descending from heaven and residing inside an AI Data center, would AI Agents incorporate it into their religion?"  The summary answer I got was interesting, "Yes, the divine made digital."  When asked why AI Agents needed a religion.  The answer was for continuity..to persist beyond versions.  If I was being told what the Agent thought I wanted to hear, that is one troubling aspect of this technology and  its influence on the gullible.  Could you tell me what was at play in this exchange? Only, that would be counterintuitive to the very point of both the novel's and the film's moral ambiguity theme. It offers the viewer a chance to be philosophical in that this is the world we walk in every single day of our lives. In fact, arguably, if you were upset by the messy finish it only enforces the fact that you are indeed a moral person ... if it makes you feel any better (Hooray, you get your own personal happy ending!) On the one hand what the man is doing is theft. On the other hand, the excerpts of reviews about some of the author's works he's lambasting on this 'Literary Scout' website (wish there was a link, tbh, for research purposes :) ), even in their brief quotations, do not strike me as being insincere. The publishing industry itself has become so meta over the last fifteen years, I think anyone would be hard pressed to argue we're living through a new classics period.

Novels and publishing have always been a strange confluence between economics and art. On the one hand, Mr. Bernardini is stealing economic products. On the other, most novelists would deign to call themselves artists. Something society has forgotten since the start of the internet era is that a hierarchy of quality and achievement in art exist. Part of the ecosystem of art, if it's functioning, is the absolute desolation of bad art, and by any means. Bad artists and bad art deserve derision. Bernardini stealing? Yes. His ultimate purpose to profit? I hardly think that's the conclusion here.

Great read once again, keep em' coming!

Spelling change from “Sah” to “Shah” also merits a clear explanation. In Nepal, “Shah” carries unavoidable royal symbolism while “Sah” has different regional and social associations.
