What troubles this reader most is how easily ordinary citizens get pushed out of this discussion. A prosecutor can upend your life. I want assurance that person was lawfully appointed—and that loyalty to the president is not the qualification that matters most.

Given the Trump administration’s record of blurring public duty and personal loyalty, the danger of corruption deserves far more scrutiny. Who gets investigated? Who gets protected? Who gets to keep the public in the dark?

Judge Cannon’s decision, for example, to block release of Jack Smith’s classified-documents report protects Trump from scrutiny while denying the rest of us information about his conduct in office. The unexplained appellate delays only deepen that failure of accountability. We don’t have to assume the report proves a crime to insist that withholding it carries a serious public cost.

I’m tired of watching accountability become negotiable when the person involved is politically powerful. Public office is a public trust. We taxpayers and voters are entitled to know how that trust was used—or abused.

comments.name: Ryan
comments.body: AI should be used in school but heavily restricted. Ai is an incredibly powerful tool and can also be a way to cheat. I think that students need to know how to use Ai while still writing and forming new thoughts. Ai should be used for finding quotes, articles, and offering grammar advice or different ways to structure a paragraph. However Ai should not be used to just think for you and write the essay itself. Sooner or later people are going to get really good at being able to tell if something is made by Ai. The people who used Ai in a way that made learning easier will thrive, the people who used Ai to cheat will not be able to write without it.

comments.name: Bernhard
comments.body: I'm a high school teacher, and I encounter a range of writing abilities, A.I. dependencies, etc. I find it interesting that the some of the students who appear to be most supportive of A.I. in this piece tend to have the weakest grammar, mechanics, thought structure etc. these are the students who need AI-free writing the most. corollation does not imply causation, but one can see the subtle, corroding effects of A.I. dependency in real time.

comments.name: Erik
comments.body: I don't know where you found all these reasonably sounding students, but I can tell you, as a university professor at a public university in Florida, that roughly 80% of my students are using generative AI to write their assignments. Probably closer to 100% in online classes, which universities started to put their money on decades ago. For many of the students, taking classes is the way to getting a degree, not necessarily to learn for life. Many of these students work one, sometimes two jobs at the same time. For them, AI is a crucial time-saver. As long as our education system is geared at producing degrees, by any means necessary, rather than focusing on the learning experience itself, this is what we will get, students cheating on a massive scale, certainly in online teaching. It's ridiculous to think otherwise. This should be the end of online teaching, but of course it won't be, because it's a massive money maker for universities.

comments.name: Lyla
comments.body: Ai in the school setting is a very complex topic to talk about. There really is so much gray area: it’s detrimental to our writing skills, yet it is our future. AI being such a prominent part of our lives is not something we can ignore. We have to recognize that we shouldn’t rely on it but we need to learn how to live with it. It’s never going to go away so there’s no use in complaining about how it’s ruining the youths writing abilities. We need to take the blame away from the youth, who were not even the ones to invent AI, and rather teach them how to use it properly. Much like in this article, I too have been in the position where I came home late, or I just had a lot going on at that moment so I turned to AI to write an assignment for me. I believe that we should help teach kids like me, and the kids featured in the article, that were not bad students for using AI, but we do need to know how to use it properly. Constantly relying on it to do all of your assignments is not using it correctly. Instead, if you come home late or whatever the circumstance may be, try asking for advice on how to write a strong essay, rather than having it skimpily write the whole thing. Then at least the ideas and the work are still coming from your own mind. We as a society must learn how to coexist with AI and not resent it or depend on it.

Good News!  I love to hear that important historical  buildings/homes are being saved.  We have a tendency to tear our history down, not save it.

Every house, like the Morris-Jumel Mansion, is important. Not just because famous people stood, sat or slept there. They show how people lived during the time of our country's founding.

I helped save The Elijah Miller House/Washington's HQ in North Castle, NY.  The house sits in the same exact spot it has been in for nearly 300 years. It was Washington's HQ during the Battle of White Plains. When Washington was able to get to Miller House, he saw he could use Miller Hill as high ground to once and for all stop the British onslaught that had chased Washington and his troops from Long Island (The Battle of L.I.) through Manhattan, the Bronx and into Westchester County.

By claiming the high ground Washington won the day, repelling British troops back for the first time. Washington later used darkness and rain to leave the British behind as he made his way to New Jersey for the winter.

Miller House is owned by Westchester County and it had fallen into disrepair. Then County Executive George Latimer found the money to fix it properly.  I hope the Morris-Jumel Mansion receives the love and care it deserves. I will look into visiting this historic sight sometime soon.

Preserving our past will help inform our future, I truly believe that.

As far as Weinstein is concerned. He deserves to die in jail. He shows no remorse. Disgusting.

While clean-energy transportation remains the ideal goal, commercial transport still relies heavily on diesel fuel, directly impacting the consumer economy.

To mitigate anxieties surrounding a potential diesel shortage, federal and state governments could prioritize the diesel supply exclusively for commercial and industrial uses. This could be achieved by levying excise taxes or special one-time fees to artificially raise pump prices for those who drive diesel pickup trucks and boats strictly for leisure and other recreational purposes, while simultaneously offering tax rebates or credits to commercial operators.

Such a mitigating measure would discourage non-essential diesel consumption and insulate the broader economy from rising costs by confining the price shock to a smaller, wealthier upper-middle-class consumer segment purchasing high-end diesel trucks and boats for recreational purposes.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
What worries me in particular about these fires is that they are turning our forests from important carbon sinks into net emitters of carbon dioxide (CO2, a greenhouse gas).

The 2023 Canadian wildfires released more CO2 than the rest of Canadian sources combined (37 million acres burned). Climate models did not project fires like that until much later this century.

And recently this paper reported that the permafrost region has shifted from an important carbon sink into a net emitter of greenhouse gases, CO2 and methane.

The huge fires in the Northern Boreal forests are also dumping black carbon on ice which increases heat retention and melt rate.

Some natural systems like forests and frozen soils which minimized some of the impacts of our atmospheric experiment with our only planet are changing from being our friends to our enemies.

Interesting article, but somewhat lacking in the 'good' things about AI in my opinion. I use AI daily, multiple times for multiple reasons. When I say this to people their immediate response is 'but AI is wrong' without hesitation. Whereas those same people believe what they read on social media. 
AI has the capacity to dig deeper and faster for material(s) than humans can. They can analze, catagorize, summarize in an instant. AI has the ability to jump subject matter and schedule tasks. 
I am currently using AI to search family history. What a time and money saver. While firewalls prevent AI from accessing Geneaology sites and Government sites, they can rapidly scan public sites that provide critical information. 
AI can evaluate products that I use, providing breakdowns say on my nutritional supplements and tell me if I'm purchasing snake oil or something beneficial. 
TV, radio, telephones, cell phones, computers and AI have all been catagorized as things that would end the world. Only when you give the power to do so.

comments.name: Mihailo Zoin
comments.body:
Have We Advanced or Regressed?

Transposed into modern times, our progress is largely procedural, masking deeper regression:

1. Little Rock (1957) vs. Today: We regressed in subtlety. While soldiers with fixed bayonets no longer guard school entrances, physical segregation has morphed into algorithmic echo chambers and digital redlining where youth are isolated into polarized ideological camps.   
2. Sequoia (1890) & UN Goals (2015) vs. Today: In 1890, cavalry was deployed directly on the ground to halt logging; today, we sign polished declarations while real destruction is offset through creative corporate accounting. The bureaucracy has advanced; genuine ecological stewardship has stalled.   
3. Bonham (1980) vs. Today: When Bonham passed away, the band dissolved out of respect for an irreplaceable human soul. Today, an AI model would simulate his drumming style in minutes to sell tickets for a hologram tour — technological advancement at the expense of human authenticity.
